$V=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The volume of a parallelepiped spanned by three vectors is given by the absolute value of their triple product.

First, we compute the triple product:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 & 6\end{aligned}| \\  & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}|+3\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 5 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(30)-2(0\cdot 6-1\cdot 4)+3(0\cdot 0-5\cdot 4) \\  & =30+8-60 \\  & =-22\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we take the absolute value. So, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped is 

$$
V=|-22|=22.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-752c7d24-ba0b-5853-99e8-14fd968c0d02"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-752c7d24-ba0b-5853-99e8-14fd968c0d02" :answer-field/id #uuid "752c7d24-ba0b-5853-99e8-14fd968c0d02" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-ef21b691-d97c-5047-bd55-f0d2f57c360d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ef21b691-d97c-5047-bd55-f0d2f57c360d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ef21b691-d97c-5047-bd55-f0d2f57c360d" :answer/id #uuid "ef21b691-d97c-5047-bd55-f0d2f57c360d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "22" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-65ad1da6-49b7-5494-8267-2eea67ec5389" :question/id #uuid "65ad1da6-49b7-5494-8267-2eea67ec5389" :question/math-academy-id "q-280747" :question/problem "Find $k$ given that the vectors $a=⟨2,k,-1⟩$, $b=⟨-3,4,5⟩$, and $c=⟨6,k,1⟩$ are coplanar.

$k=${{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}2 & k & -1 \\ -3 & 4 & 5 \\ 6 & k & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ k & 1\end{aligned}|-k\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 5 \\ 6 & 1\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & 4 \\ 6 & k\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(4\cdot 1-5\cdot k)-k(-3\cdot 1-5\cdot 6)-1(-3\cdot k-4\cdot 6) \\  & =8-10k+33k+3k+24 \\  & =26k+32\end{aligned}
$$

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =0 \\ 26k+32 & =0 \\ k & =-\frac{16}{13}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $k=-\frac{16}{13}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aefbe563-901b-5005-9895-d7c05a2acfbf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-aefbe563-901b-5005-9895-d7c05a2acfbf" :answer-field/id #uuid "aefbe563-901b-5005-9895-d7c05a2acfbf" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-eea5ea1b-1584-5bf8-9c56-60e082cc3b30" :answer-field/choices ["answer-eea5ea1b-1584-5bf8-9c56-60e082cc3b30"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-eea5ea1b-1584-5bf8-9c56-60e082cc3b30" :answer/id #uuid "eea5ea1b-1584-5bf8-9c56-60e082cc3b30" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{13}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106095 :question/problem "Find $t$ given that the vectors $p=⟨3,t,t⟩$, $q=⟨1,3,1⟩$, and $r=⟨1,1,3⟩$ are coplanar." :question/worked-solution "Computing the triple product, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =|\begin{aligned}3 & t & t \\ 1 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|-t\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|+t\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =3(3\cdot 3-1\cdot 1)-t(1\cdot 3-1\cdot 1)+t(1\cdot 1-3\cdot 1) \\  & =24-2t-2t \\  & =24-4t.\end{aligned}
$$

    

Three vectors are coplanar if and only if their triple product is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}p\cdot (q\times r) & =0 \\ 24-4t & =0 \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the three vectors are coplanar if and only if $t=6.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186102446 :answer-field/correct 17592186102450 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186106044 :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC}$ and $\overset{\to }{AD},$ given the points $A(9,6,1),$ $B(9,7,2),$ $C(7,5,2),$ and $D(7,8,3).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find the displacement vectors $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ that span the parallelepiped:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =b-a \\  & =(9i+7j+2k)-(9i+6j+k) \\  & =j+k \\  & =⟨0,1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AC} & =c-a \\  & =(7i+5j+2k)-(9i+6j+k) \\  & =-2i-j+k \\  & =⟨-2,-1,1⟩ \\ \overset{\to }{AD} & =d-a \\  & =(7i+8j+3k)-(9i+6j+k) \\  & =-2i+2j+2k \\  & =⟨-2,2,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the volume of the parallelepiped, we need to take the absolute value of the triple product of the above vectors.

Computing the triple product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB}\cdot (\overset{\to }{AC}\times \overset{\to }{AD}) & =|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & -1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =0\cdot |\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}|-1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}|+1\cdot |\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =0-((-2)\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot 1)+((-2)\cdot 2-(-2)\cdot (-1)) \\  & =2-6 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the corresponding parallelepiped spanned by $\overset{\to }{AB},$ $\overset{\to }{AC},$ and $\overset{\to }{AD}$ is

$$
V=|-4|=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186102150 :answer-field/correct 17592186102155 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119838 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-12b4f5c6-720f-5c2c-b1e8-295eb7dcb29c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120290 :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:\{\begin{aligned}x=5-2t \\ y=-1+4t \\ z=-3-5t\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,Π:2x-5y+3z-84=0.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can substitute the parametric expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ of the line into the equation of the plane immediately:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-5y+3z-84 & =0 \\ 2(5-2t)-5(-1+4t)+3(-3-5t) & =84 \\ 10-4t+5-20t-9-15t & =84 \\ -39t & =78 \\ t & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=-2$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=5-2(-2)=9 \\ y=-1+4(-2)=-9 \\ z=-3-5(-2)=7\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is  $P(9,-9,7).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-12b4f5c6-720f-5c2c-b1e8-295eb7dcb29c" :question/id #uuid "12b4f5c6-720f-5c2c-b1e8-295eb7dcb29c" :question/math-academy-id "q-73991" :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:\{\begin{aligned}x=-2-2t \\ y=5-3t \\ z=-1+2t\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,Π:3x-2y+6z=62.
$$" :question/worked-solution "We can substitute the parametric expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ of the line into the equation of the plane immediately:

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-2y+6z & =62 \\ 3(-2-2t)-2(5-3t)+6(-1+2t) & =62 \\ -6-6t-10+6t-6+12t & =62 \\ 12t & =84 \\ t & =7\end{aligned}
$$

To get the position vector $p$ of the intersection point $P$, we substitute $t=6$ into the parametric equations of the line:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2-2(7)=-16 \\ y=5-3(7)=-16 \\ z=-1+2(7)=13\end{aligned}
$$

So, the intersection point is $P(-16,-16,13).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-15f90597-4c03-5ae4-b2c2-f42eae091087"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-15f90597-4c03-5ae4-b2c2-f42eae091087" :answer-field/id #uuid "15f90597-4c03-5ae4-b2c2-f42eae091087" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-20fc86f8-0368-54eb-a3e0-3cf6b0379332" :answer-field/choices ["answer-20fc86f8-0368-54eb-a3e0-3cf6b0379332" "answer-7944f3e7-3b31-5e5a-b5cb-a1562208eb42" "answer-2143e54b-67d5-5002-957a-3bf88c230ca4" "answer-a0a4f2b9-c6e0-5e67-8ab6-66d592472d45" "answer-257b548a-b52d-5b2d-8a2f-57d74b50d39c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20fc86f8-0368-54eb-a3e0-3cf6b0379332" :answer/id #uuid "20fc86f8-0368-54eb-a3e0-3cf6b0379332" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-16,-16,13)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7944f3e7-3b31-5e5a-b5cb-a1562208eb42" :answer/id #uuid "7944f3e7-3b31-5e5a-b5cb-a1562208eb42" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(11,-13,11)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2143e54b-67d5-5002-957a-3bf88c230ca4" :answer/id #uuid "2143e54b-67d5-5002-957a-3bf88c230ca4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(24,-11,11)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0a4f2b9-c6e0-5e67-8ab6-66d592472d45" :answer/id #uuid "a0a4f2b9-c6e0-5e67-8ab6-66d592472d45" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(26,12,12)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-257b548a-b52d-5b2d-8a2f-57d74b50d39c" :answer/id #uuid "257b548a-b52d-5b2d-8a2f-57d74b50d39c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No intersection" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186342127 :question/problem "Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

"88299f24-4f45-5ffe-aaf6-eeca4cfa5124" :question/math-academy-id "q-75089" :question/problem "The matrix $P$ is given below. Let ${p}_{1}$, ${p}_{2}$,  ${p}_{3}$ and ${p}_{4}$ be the respective columns of $P.$ Determine if $B=\text{{}{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(P).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${p}_{4}={x}_{1}{p}_{1}+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we reduce the matrix $P$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(P)$ is $\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $4$th column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${p}_{4}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{4}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{1}}+{{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{p}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 2=4.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-259644ac-e832-5d7b-b706-9bf284412c4b"] :db/ensure "4e023a9e-c79a-53ca-9a76-a188bd7ab902" :question/math-academy-id "q-75951" :question/problem "The matrix $Q$ is given below. Let ${q}_{1}$, ${q}_{2}$, and ${q}_{3}$ be the respective columns of $Q.$
Determine if $B=\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\text{}}$ is a basis of $\text{Col}(Q).$ 
If that is the case, find ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}$, where ${q}_{3}={x}_{1}{q}_{1}+{x}_{2}{q}_{2}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we reduce the matrix $Q$ to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned}Q & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

From the matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$ is $\{{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\},$ that is to say,

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Now, since the $3$rd column of the reduced matrix is a non-pivot column, then the entries in that column tell us the coefficients needed to express ${q}_{3}$ as a linear combination of all the other columns in the original matrix. So, we have

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{3}}={{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{1}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{1}}+{{(2)}_{⏟}}_{{x}_{2}}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{q}_{2}}.
$$

This gives us ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}=2\cdot 2=4.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-64759caf-77ed-5792-a395-f9662dbea5af"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-64759caf-77ed-5792-a395-f9662dbea5af" :answer-field/id #uuid "64759caf-77ed-5792-a395-f9662dbea5af" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-12117f66-7e89-5080-9c67-2baf0fc5322d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4c340483-1504-5c29-8184-e2464a93b17c" "answer-7ecb7b58-6f98-517c-8a10-0c822f40ce2c" "answer-b17ad927-4efe-5a54-8fec-c33efe368201" "answer-12117f66-7e89-5080-9c67-2baf0fc5322d" "answer-b5f2c10c-efb5-5f13-bc42-613ef41e630b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4c340483-1504-5c29-8184-e2464a93b17c" :answer/id #uuid "4c340483-1504-5c29-8184-e2464a93b17c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ecb7b58-6f98-517c-8a10-0c822f40ce2c" :answer/id #uuid "7ecb7b58-6f98-517c-8a10-0c822f40ce2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b17ad927-4efe-5a54-8fec-c33efe368201" :answer/id #uuid "b17ad927-4efe-5a54-8fec-c33efe368201" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-12117f66-7e89-5080-9c67-2baf0fc5322d" :answer/id #uuid "12117f66-7e89-5080-9c67-2baf0fc5322d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b5f2c10c-efb5-5f13-bc42-613ef41e630b" :answer/id #uuid "b5f2c10c-efb5-5f13-bc42-613ef41e630b" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$\text{{}{q}_{1},{q}_{2}\text{}}$ is not a basis of $\text{Col}(Q)$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-eb27e567-0848-5034-b8d8-32b6b421d46e" :question/id #uuid "eb27e567-0848-5034-b8d8-32b6b421d46e" :question/math-academy-id "q-111504" :question/problem "The matrix $H$ is given below. $$

$$

$$
\dfrac{1}{(2y)^{1/3}} = (2y)^{-1/3}
$$

$$
\dfrac{1}{\sqrt[3\phantom{|}]{2y}} = (2y)^{-1/3}

\frac{1}{\sqrt[9]{t}}={t}^{-1/9}

power notation." :question/worked-solution "First, we convert the radical to a fractional exponent:

$$

$$

 

Then, we take the reciprocal and convert the exponent to a negative exponent:

$$

$$

$$

Similarly,

- a cube root such as $\sqrt[{\color{blue}3\!\phantom{p}}]{x}$ is equivalent to $x^{1/\color{blue}{3}},$

- a tenth root $\sqrt[{\color{blue}10\!\phantom{p}}]{x}$ is equivalent to $x^{1/\color{blue}{10}},$

and so on. In general, we have the following formula:

$$
\sqrt[n]{x} = x^{1/n}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068928 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119948 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-92ddc7e5-b6d3-5672-8ade-2787d57915e1" "question-a7e2dc04-d285-5815-98e3-c99d4176897c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-92ddc7e5-b6d3-5672-8ade-2787d57915e1" :question/id #uuid "92ddc7e5-b6d3-5672-8ade-2787d57915e1" :question/math-academy-id "q-132014" :question/problem "Using the cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨t,\,{e}^{-t}⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-{e}^{-t}⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-{e}^{-t})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{e}^{-2t}+1} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}{{e}^{t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{e}^{-t})⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,{e}^{-t}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =⟨1,\,-{e}^{-t},\,0⟩\times ⟨0,\,{e}^{-t},\,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & -{e}^{-t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-t} & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}1 & -{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & ={e}^{-t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖={e}^{-t}.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-t}}{{(\frac{\sqrt{{e}^{2t}+1}}{{e}^{t}})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-t}}{(\frac{\sqrt{{({e}^{2t}+1)}^{3}}}{{e}^{3t}})} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{2t}+1)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-795c37b4-5f92-5e3b-aa83-2f9b29aa6f03"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id cross product curvature formula, find the curvature of $r(t)=⟨4{t}^{2},\,4t⟩$ as a function of $t.$" :question/worked-solution "The curvature $κ$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}}.
$$

First, we calculate ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4{t}^{2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨8t,\,4⟩ \\  & =4⟨2t,\,1⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =4\sqrt{(2t)^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =4\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the second derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{″}(t) & =4⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =4⟨2,\,0⟩ \\  & =8⟨1,\,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute the cross product by considering ${r}^{′}(t)$ and ${r}^{″}(t)$ as $3$-dimensional vectors with zero $z$-components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t) & =(4⟨2t,\,1,\,0⟩)\times (8⟨1,\,0,\,0⟩) \\  & =32\,\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2t & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =32\,\left|\begin{aligned}2t & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right|\,k \\  & =-32\,k\end{aligned}
$$

So, the magnitude of the cross product is

$$
‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖=32.
$$

Therefore, the curvature is

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{‖{r}^{′}(t)\times {r}^{″}(t)‖}{‖{r}^{′}(t){‖}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{32}{{(4\sqrt{4{t}^{2}+1})}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{32}{64\sqrt{{(4{t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{{(4{t}^{2}+1)}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-32a2621c-52bf-54ef-b979-b5a1bacfe6d6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{121}$ be a random sample of size $n=121$ from a population with a population mean $\mu =300$ and population standard deviation $\sigma =55.$ Find an approximation for the probability that the sample mean is less than $295.$

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,-1.0\,$ | $\,0.1587\,$ | $\,0.1562\,$ | $\,0.1539\,$ |
| $\,-0.9\,$ | $\,0.1841\,$ | $\,0.1814\,$ | $\,0.1788\,$ |
| $\,-0.8\,$ | $\,0.2119\,$ | $\,0.2090\,$ | $\,0.2061\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with a population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
n=121,\,\mu =300,\,\sigma =55.
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(300,\frac{{55}^{2}}{121}) \\  & ∼N(300,25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<295).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =P(Z<\frac{295-300}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & =P(Z<-\frac{5}{5}) \\  & =P(Z<-1) \\  & =Φ(-1)\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(-1)=0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<295) & =Φ(-1) \\  & =0.1587.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cd48dcdf-ec5c-553b-93df-1ad0ce12e474"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id </tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =30,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}x\cdot (\frac{2}{3}-\frac{2}{15}x)\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{2x}{3}-\frac{2}{15}{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{45}]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =(\frac{16}{3}-\frac{128}{45})-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{2}{45}) \\  & =\frac{11}{5} \\  & =2.2,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.66.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(2.2,\frac{0.66}{30}) \\  & ∼N(2.2,0.022).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =P(\frac{2-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}<Z<\frac{2.3-2.2}{\sqrt{0.022}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.35<Z<0.67) \\  & =P(Z<0.67)-P(Z<-1.35) \\  & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35)\end{aligned}
$$

From the tables, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ(0.67)=0.7486, \\ Φ(-1.35)=0.0885.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(2<\overset{―}{X}<2.3) & =Φ(0.67)-Φ(-1.35) \\  & =0.7486-0.0885 \\  & =0.6601.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aa4e5556-e66f-5ee1-bddc-c98cca0920b9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-aa4e5556-e66f-5ee1-bddc-c98cca0920b9" :answer-field/id #uuid "aa4e5556-e66f-5ee1-bddc-c98cca0920b9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-da0abab7-344b-5db3-b96e-606236a85502" :answer-field/choices ["answer-40ba174f-6f4c-59fc-b3cb-137e1297aa50" "answer-82de29c2-442b-50b3-b8a2-f2cef0536930" "answer-554630d6-0001-5d34-98b7-ae518e793543" "answer-da0abab7-344b-5db3-b96e-606236a85502" "answer-e46f85da-0699-50b2-9c52-f46103534b9a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-40ba174f-6f4c-59fc-b3cb-137e1297aa50" :answer/id #uuid "40ba174f-6f4c-59fc-b3cb-137e1297aa50" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5429" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-82de29c2-442b-50b3-b8a2-f2cef0536930" :answer/id #uuid "82de29c2-442b-50b3-b8a2-f2cef0536930" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.5678" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-554630d6-0001-5d34-98b7-ae518e793543" :answer/id #uuid "554630d6-0001-5d34-98b7-ae518e793543" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6112" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-da0abab7-344b-5db3-b96e-606236a85502" :answer/id #uuid "da0abab7-344b-5db3-b96e-606236a85502" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.6601" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e46f85da-0699-50b2-9c52-f46103534b9a" :answer/id #uuid "e46f85da-0699-50b2-9c52-f46103534b9a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.7123" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064506 :question/problem "Let ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{25}$ be a random sample of size $n=25$ from a population with probability density function

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =25,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{3}{8}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3}{8}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3{x}^{4}}{32}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3}{2} \\  & =1.5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is ${\sigma }^{2}=0.15.$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(1.5,\frac{0.15}{25}) \\  & ∼N(1.5,0.006).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =P(Z>\frac{1.6-1.5}{\sqrt{0.006}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>1.29)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the complement of the normal distribution, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Z>1.29) & =1-P(Z<1.29) \\  & =1-Φ(1.29).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, we have

$$
Φ(1.29)=0.9015.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}>1.6) & =1-Φ(1.29) \\  & =1-0.9015 \\  & =0.0985.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186061266 :answer-field/correct 17592186061267 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064314 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-5574158c-e378-5c22-867d-7f3ecb6e0b26" "question-a7a75f10-4331-5d53-8955-dd0d91fe7458"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-5574158c-e378-5c22-867d-7f3ecb6e0b26" :question/id #uuid "5574158c-e378-5c22-867d-7f3ecb6e0b26" :question/math-academy-id "q-143513" :question/problem "| $x$ | $0$ | $5$ | $10$ | $15$ |

*Note: $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ is a random sample of size $n$ from a population with population mean $\mu $ and population standard deviation $\sigma .$ The central limit theorem (or CLT) states that for sufficiently large $n,$ the distribution of the sample mean $\overset{―}{X}$ can be approximated as 

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=116,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =0\cdot 0.6+5\cdot 0.1+10\cdot 0.2+15\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0+0.5+2+1.5 \\  & =4,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =({0}^{2}\cdot 0.6+{5}^{2}\cdot 0.1+{10}^{2}\cdot 0.2+{15}^{2}\cdot 0.1)-{4}^{2} \\  & =(0+2.5+20+22.5)-16 \\  & =29.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(4,\frac{29}{116}) \\  & ∼N(4,0.25).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5) & ≈P(\frac{3-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}<Z<\frac{5-4}{\sqrt{0.25}}) \\  & =P(-2<Z<2) \\  & =Φ(2)-Φ(-2).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(3<\overset{―}{X}<5)=Φ(2)-Φ(-2).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9247b964-7703-5bda-8b8b-02af0509ca08"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9247b964-7703-5bda-8b8b-02af0509ca08" :answer-field/id #uuid "9247b964-7703-5bda-8b8b-02af0509ca08" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-900ec749-ed02-5243-a1b6-eea5f267a77c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ecf42980-f617-5f97-b30d-0955b76d372f" "answer-58e231ce-e2dc-5918-a3f7-c22726470c58" "answer-c02cc025-e442-50e2-9860-12b5a1a52c28" "answer-900ec749-ed02-5243-a1b6-eea5f267a77c" "answer-b9fe1f0e-03f6-5c1b-9efa-37601b693f09"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ecf42980-f617-5f97-b30d-0955b76d372f" :answer/id #uuid "ecf42980-f617-5f97-b30d-0955b76d372f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Φ(1)-Φ(-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-58e231ce-e2dc-5918-a3f7-c22726470c58" :answer/id #uuid "58e231ce-e2dc-5918-a3f7-c22726470c58" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Φ(1)-Φ(-1.5)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c02cc025-e442-50e2-9860-12b5a1a52c28" :answer/id #uuid "c02cc025-e442-50e2-9860-12b5a1a52c28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Φ(1.5)-Φ(-1.5)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-900ec749-ed02-5243-a1b6-eea5f267a77c" :answer/id #uuid "900ec749-ed02-5243-a1b6-eea5f267a77c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Φ(2)-Φ(-2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b9fe1f0e-03f6-5c1b-9efa-37601b693f09" :answer/id #uuid "b9fe1f0e-03f6-5c1b-9efa-37601b693f09" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "Φ(2.5)-Φ(-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a7a75f10-4331-5d53-8955-dd0d91fe7458" :question/id #uuid "a7a75f10-4331-5d53-8955-dd0d91fe7458" :question/math-academy-id "q-143514" :question/problem "| $x$ | $-8$ | $-6$ | $-4$ | $-2$ |

$$
\overset{―}{X}∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}).
$$

In our case:

- the sample size is 

$$
n=65,
$$

- the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\text{E}[X] \\  & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{x}_{i}f({x}_{i}) \\  & =(-8)\cdot 0.1+(-6)\cdot 0.4+(-4)\cdot 0.4+(-2)\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.8-2.4-1.6-0.2 \\  & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

- the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\text{Var}[X] \\  & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =((-8)^{2}\cdot 0.1+(-6)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-4)^{2}\cdot 0.4+(-2)^{2}\cdot 0.1)-(-5)^{2} \\  & =(6.4+14.4+6.4+0.4)-25 \\  & =2.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the CLT, we have that the distribution of the sample mean can be approximated as

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{X} & ∼N\,(\mu ,\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}) \\  & ∼N\,(-5,\frac{2.6}{65}) \\  & ∼N(-5,0.04).\end{aligned}
$$

We want to find $P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9).$ So, we convert $\overset{―}{X}$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9) & ≈P(Z<\frac{-4.9-(-5)}{\sqrt{0.04}}) \\  & =P(Z<0.5) \\  & =Φ(0.5).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
P(\overset{―}{X}<-4.9)=Φ(0.5).

"cd425a39-318f-5566-a2e2-b27e6f8eab87" :question/math-academy-id "q-223098" :question/problem "$$
T(t)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩.
$$

The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given above. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$N(t)=$
$⟨$
{{field-1}},

$\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩ \\  & =2⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =2‖⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩‖ \\  & =2\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t))}^{2}+{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(2t)} \\  & =2\sqrt{1} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{2⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩}{2} \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-28d3585e-134e-53e5-b3ff-d54d2085a716"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-28d3585e-134e-53e5-b3ff-d54d2085a716" :answer-field/id #uuid "28d3585e-134e-53e5-b3ff-d54d2085a716" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-9c0bb344-e2e7-53b7-a86b-a70876c813ac" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9c0bb344-e2e7-53b7-a86b-a70876c813ac"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9c0bb344-e2e7-53b7-a86b-a70876c813ac" :answer/id #uuid "9c0bb344-e2e7-53b7-a86b-a70876c813ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\cos(2t)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186289935 :answer-field/correct "answer-099d7c1b-7772-5cc6-9777-a7e269acac3d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-099d7c1b-7772-5cc6-9777-a7e269acac3d"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-099d7c1b-7772-5cc6-9777-a7e269acac3d" :answer/id #uuid "099d7c1b-7772-5cc6-9777-a7e269acac3d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sin(t+1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-34386db1-c26a-52c0-8482-81ad51998468" :question/id #uuid "34386db1-c26a-52c0-8482-81ad51998468" :question/math-academy-id "q-358781" :question/problem "$$
T(t)=\frac{1}{5}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-4\,k).
$$

The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given above. Find the principal normal vector to that curve at an arbitrary point on the curve.

$N(t)=$
{{field-1}}
$i\,+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{5}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i-3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j-4\,k)) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4)\,k) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(t)‖ & =\frac{3}{5}‖\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j‖ \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(t)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j)}{\frac{3}{5}} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-83efe503-c6c7-5398-8b5a-e3c31636860c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $9x^2+30x+25.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
a^2 + {\color{red}{2}}a{\color{blue}{b}} + {\color{blue}b}^2 =  (a+{\color{blue}{b}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
9x^2+30x+25.
$$

First, we write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}+30x+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}+2(15x)+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the middle parentheses $(15x)$ as a product of $3x$ and ${\color{blue}5}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}+2(3x\cdot 5)+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=3x$ and ${\color{blue}{b}} = {\color{blue}{5}}.$ This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}(3x+5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068902 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f1a4e854-18be-5044-a0a8-f098474cee63" "question-8c53c9a4-fe1b-5044-8911-e4ffad0659c2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068520 :question/problem "Factor $9y^2-12y+4.$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$
a^2 - {\color{red}{2}}a{\color{blue}{b}} + {\color{blue}b}^2 =  (a-{\color{blue}{b}})^2 .
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
9y^2-12y+4.
$$

First, we write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3y)^{2}-12y+(2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3y)^{2}-2(6y)+(2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the middle parentheses $(6y)$ as a product of $3y$ and ${\color{blue}2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3y)^{2}-2(3y\cdot 2)+(2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula with $a=3y$ and ${\color{blue}{b}} = {\color{blue}{2}}.$ This gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}(3y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068848 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-388f80cd-cabc-537e-b7cd-20f266912f80"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068465 :question/problem "Factor the expression $7a^2+28a+28.$" :question/worked-solution "Before we start our normal process of factoring, notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $7.$ Therefore, we can simplify the expression by factoring out $7,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{a}^{2}+28a+28 & = \\ 7({a}^{2}+4a+4)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's factor the expression inside parentheses using the square of sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+4a+4 & = \\ {a}^{2}+4a+{2}^{2} \\ {a}^{2}+2\cdot 2a+{2}^{2} \\ (a+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}7({a}^{2}+4a+4) & = \\ 7(a+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068849 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e1247d09-04db-57b2-b09e-dc5dafe32a21" "question-66f132c4-a82c-5cf3-bd20-df4c38d0e1c3" "question-f2d099da-828c-5882-bf9e-a7fe2ace1301" "question-fa78e3d6-5bc5-5702-a92b-18645aa6667d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068466 :question/problem "Factor ![](images/a0/a026f57159735d92a77f9fe46f17720e60e27081143e9fa0e128a69ca1e56687.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is negative. ![](images/a0/a0fc84a06635785af990620d5d671329588a8018c0e0cdbc6beb130a23596070.svg)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-fbd5a08f-884b-5546-b21c-f131de083119" :question/id #uuid "fbd5a08f-884b-5546-b21c-f131de083119" :question/math-academy-id "q-31972" :question/problem "$9{b}^{2}+24b+16=$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
{a}^{2}+2ab+{b}^{2}=(a+b)^{2}.
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
9{p}^{2}+30p+25.
$$

First, we write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3p)^{2}+30p+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

$$
\begin{aligned}(3p)^{2}+2(15p)+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the middle parentheses $(15p)$ as a product of $3p$ and $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3p)^{2}+2(3p\cdot 5)+(5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of a sum formula with $a=3p$ and $b=5.$ This gives

$$
4x^2+12x+9
$$

has a leading coefficient of $4,$ and it is a perfect square trinomial because it is the square of the binomial $(2x+3)$ as we can see below:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+3)^{2} & = \\ (2x)^{2}+2(2x)(3)+(3)^{2} & = \\ 4{x}^{2}+12x+9 & \end{aligned}
$$

To factor a perfect square trinomial with a leading coefficient other than $1,$ we use the square of sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+2ab+{b}^{2} & =(a+b)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $4x^2+12x+9$ using the square of sum formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+12x+9 & = \\ (2x)^{2}+12x+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x)^{2}+2(6x)+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Write the middle parentheses $(6x)$ as a product of $2x$ and ${\color{blue}3}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x)^{2}+2(2x\cdot 3)+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

4\. Factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula. In this case, we have $a=2x$ and $b=3\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

**Note:** This method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial. But we will learn more general methods in the future." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069954 :tutorial/content "Other perfect square trinomials can be factored as the square of a difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}-2ab+{b}^{2} & =(a-b)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $9x^2-24x+16$ using the square of difference formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-24x+16 & = \\ (3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Write the middle parentheses $(12x)$ as a product of $3x$ and ${\color{blue}4}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

4\. Factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula. In this case, we have $a=3x$ and $b=4\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x-4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

**Note:** Once again, we note that this method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069941 :tutorial/content "How can we factor a trinomial that has a negative leading coefficient, like

$$
-25y^2 + 20y - 4\,?
$$

 
We can reduce this to a more familiar problem by factoring out $−1$ from the entire expression:

$$

\begin{aligned}25{y}^{2}-20y+4 & = \\ (5y)^{2}-20y+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(10y)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(5y\cdot 2)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y-2)^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-(25{y}^{2}-20y+4) & = \\ -(5y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}

For example, the cube root of $8$ is $2$ since 

$$
2^3 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8,
$$

and the cube root of $-8$ is $-2$ since

$$
(-2)^3 = (-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8.
$$

In general, the cube root of $x^3$ is $x.$

Like the square root, the cube root is signified by a radical symbol, but it also has a little $3$ next to it, i.e., $\sqrt[3\!\phantom{p}]{\phantom{2}}.$ Using this notation, we can express the above statements mathematically:

- "The cube root of $8$ is $2$" can be expressed as $\sqrt[3]{8}=2.$

- "The cube root of $-8$ is $-2$" can be expressed as  $\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2.$

- "The cube root of $x^3$ is $x$" can be expressed as  $\sqrt[3]{x^3}=x.$

**Note:** For square roots, we have $\sqrt{x^2} = |x|,$ but for cube roots, we have $\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x.$ No absolute value is needed for cube roots, because

- the cube root of a positive number is a positive number, and

- the cube root of a negative number is a negative number." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068929 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186197858 :answer-field/choices 17592186197859] [:db/retract 17592186197858 :answer-field/choices 17592186197860] [:db/retract 17592186197858 :answer-field/choices 17592186197861] [:db/retract 17592186197858 :answer-field/choices 17592186197862] [:db/retract 17592186197858 :answer-field/choices 17592186197863] [:db/retract 17592186197834 :answer-field/choices 17592186197835] [:db/retract 17592186197834 :answer-field/choices 17592186197836] [:db/retract 17592186197834 :answer-field/choices 17592186197837] [:db/retract 17592186197834 :answer-field/choices 17592186197838] [:db/retract 17592186197834 :answer-field/choices 17592186197839] {:db/id 17592186198349 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-01982d7c-8631-5513-adcd-2dc3bb87a98b" "question-83fca566-7995-55f0-a5c4-c64563aea218" "question-bf7120f6-4fae-5d19-b842-ba88886669a0" "question-7819f027-d28d-5660-b11c-cd0f95f720fe"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198228 :question/problem "Find the point(s) of the intersection of the ellipsoid $\dfrac{x^2}{24} + \dfrac{y^2}{24} +\dfrac{z^2}{6} = 1$ and the line

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$" :question/worked-solution "Substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain the following:

$$

$$

Hence, we get the solution $t = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\dfrac 1 2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(-\frac{1}{2})=-2 \\ y=8(-\frac{1}{2})=-4 \\ z=2(-\frac{1}{2})=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $\left(-2,-4,-1\right).$

- For $t=\dfrac 1 2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=4(\frac{1}{2})=2 \\ y=8(\frac{1}{2})=4 \\ z=2(\frac{1}{2})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $\left(2,4,1\right).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-2,-4,-1)$ and $(2,4,1).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198433 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-03ac4047-3b67-5e2f-8026-813b5d163c02" "question-04b22284-5add-5373-b896-4f7022795490" "question-925fed75-7149-58ca-b2ab-03e5b43ab0a5" "question-54e46f90-207e-55ef-98ea-cffcdc18e2c7"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198075 :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

:question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
x-2=y+1=\frac{z}{3}=t\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=t+2 \\ y=t-1 \\ z=3t,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ 2(t+2)^{2}+4(t-1)^{2} & =(3t)^{2} \\ 2({t}^{2}+4t+4)+4({t}^{2}-2t+1) & =9{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+8t+8+4{t}^{2}-8t+4 & =9{t}^{2} \\ 3{t}^{2}-12 & =0 \\ 3({t}^{2}-4) & =0 \\ 3(t+2)(t-2) & =0 \\ t & =\pm 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=-2+2=0 \\ y=-2-1=-3 \\ z=3(-2)=-6,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(0,-3,-6).$

- For $t=2,$ we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=2+2=4 \\ y=2-1=1 \\ z=3(2)=6,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(4,1,6).$

:question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x.$ First, we solve for $x$ in the equation of the plane, as follows:

$$
x+y=2\,⟹\,x=2-y
$$

Substituting the expression for $x$ into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}(2-y)^{2}+3{y}^{2} & =6z-6 \\ {y}^{2}-4y+4+3{y}^{2} & =6z-6 \\ 6z-6 & =4{y}^{2}-4y+4 \\ 6z-6 & =4({y}^{2}-y+1) \\ 6z-6 & =4{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+3 \\ 6z & =4{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+9 \\ z & =\frac{2}{3}{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the parabola $z=\frac{2}{3}{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{3}{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "z=\frac{3}{2}{(y-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find the points of intersection of the elliptic paraboloid 
$z=x^2+y^2$
and the line with the equation
$x = -y = -z+1.$
The line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.

![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)

 

The trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.

So, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

![](images/01/01357a5c6b72d7c976765aeed04db8afa3e3a80e13095d9be1ea2f2594ae5bf5.svg)

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Our intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation, we get

$$
2t^2+t - 1=0.
$$

The solutions to this equation are
$t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 

Substituting these values back into the parametric equations of the line

- For $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ y=-(\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2} \\ z=-(\frac{1}{2})+1=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=-(-1)=1 \\ z=-(-1)+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,1,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,1,2).$ 

Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186199499 :tutorial/content "Now, let's consider the intersection of the elliptic paraboloid

I. $A$ has a zero row/column

II. $A$ has two identical rows/columns

III. $A$ has two proportional rows/columns

IV. $A$ has a row/column that is a linear combination of other rows/columns

Notice that condition IV encompasses each of the conditions I, II, and III. If we have a zero row/column, two identical rows/columns, or proportional rows/columns, then the rows/columns form a linearly dependent set of vectors. 
In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

**Watch out!** While all of the above conditions are *sufficient* to conclude that $\det(A)=0,$ only condition IV is *necessary* to conclude that $\det(A)=0.$ 
In other words, if we have a matrix $A$ with $\det(A)=0,$ then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV *must* be satisfied. 

So, we have the following theorem:

*$\det(A)=0$ if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

Finally, note also that in the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix *only*, statements III and IV mean the same thing." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186073879 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d691d9e9-ebc4-5231-9220-d7666a1593ac" "question-98f6bb07-5c0b-539a-985d-169696ff401a" "question-6e29d990-90ac-50f9-be81-d4fdf354bbe5"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d691d9e9-ebc4-5231-9220-d7666a1593ac" :question/id #uuid "d691d9e9-ebc4-5231-9220-d7666a1593ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-60243" :question/problem "What is missing in the following sentence?

$$
(0,2),\,(2,0),\,(0,0),\,(1,1).
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,2) & =2(0)^{2}+(2)^{2}-4(0)-2(2) \\  & =4-4 \\  & =0 \\ f(2,0) & =2(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(2)-2(0) \\  & =8-8 \\  & =0 \\ f(0,0) & =2(0)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(0)-2(0) \\  & =0 \\ f(1,1) & =2(1)^{2}+(1)^{2}-4(1)-2(1) \\  & =2+1-4-2 \\  & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that

"question-126e0a3b-1df5-561d-b629-66be47834dfa" :question/id #uuid "126e0a3b-1df5-561d-b629-66be47834dfa" :question/math-academy-id "q-90529" :question/problem "Given that $X$ is a continuous random $$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2x-4,\, & 2\le x\le 3, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

First, we compute $\text{E}[X]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & ={\int }_{2}^{3}x\cdot (2x-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}(2{x}^{2}-4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-2{x}^{2})|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}]:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{2}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot (2x-4)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{3}(2{x}^{3}-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})|}_{2}^{3} \\  & =\frac{43}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{43}{6}-{(\frac{8}{3})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{18}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f9a9aeae-7475-58db-b6eb-574c342ffd6f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ stated below. Given that $\text{E}[X]=1.9,$ compute $\text{Var}[X].$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}2{x}^{3}, & 0<x<1, \\ \frac{1}{8}, & 1\le x<5, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot 2{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{5}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{5}\frac{{x}^{2}}{8}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{6}}{3}|}_{0}^{1}+{\frac{{x}^{3}}{24}|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =5.5\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =5.5-{(1.9)}^{2} \\  & =1.89.\end{aligned}

Given that $\text{E}[X]=4$ compute $\text{Var}[X].$ 

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{27}, & 0<x<3, \\ \frac{9-x}{27}, & 3\le x<9, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a continuous random variable $X$ with probability density function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S,$ we can calculate the variance using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{9}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{9}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{2x}{27}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{9}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{27}(9-x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{2{x}^{3}}{27}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{3}^{9}\frac{1}{27}(9{x}^{2}-{x}^{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{4}}{54}|}_{0}^{3}+{\frac{1}{27}(3{x}^{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})|}_{3}^{9} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+\frac{81}{4}-\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{39}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the variance is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{39}{2}-{4}^{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f6082ae9-a37f-5a6d-98af-d4b226bb7c29"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f6082ae9-a37f-5a6d-98af-d4b226bb7c29" :answer-field/id #uuid "f6082ae9-a37f-5a6d-98af-d4b226bb7c29" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-325fa17b-54bd-5aa0-9e67-721dd15642fd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2b2b313e-b6a7-568c-a875-f9db4ce39dcb" "answer-6d4e985e-cf6f-56bf-aaa1-935086b1d3e4" "answer-f1f6ae5c-8838-54ee-bde6-979554af985b" "answer-5a881950-5b53-5733-8066-0e2b41f6af6d" "answer-325fa17b-54bd-5aa0-9e67-721dd15642fd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2b2b313e-b6a7-568c-a875-f9db4ce39dcb" :answer/id #uuid "2b2b313e-b6a7-568c-a875-f9db4ce39dcb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "16" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d4e985e-cf6f-56bf-aaa1-935086b1d3e4" :answer/id #uuid "6d4e985e-cf6f-56bf-aaa1-935086b1d3e4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "39" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f1f6ae5c-8838-54ee-bde6-979554af985b" :answer/id #uuid "f1f6ae5c-8838-54ee-bde6-979554af985b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{31}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a881950-5b53-5733-8066-0e2b41f6af6d" :answer/id #uuid "5a881950-5b53-5733-8066-0e2b41f6af6d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{39}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-325fa17b-54bd-5aa0-9e67-721dd15642fd" :answer/id #uuid "325fa17b-54bd-5aa0-9e67-721dd15642fd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ce424fe3-1289-5449-b3af-c9a36901436b" :question/id #uuid "ce424fe3-1289-5449-b3af-c9a36901436b" :question/math-academy-id "q-131166" :question/problem "The continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x)$ stated below. $$

 

We compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}],$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3(x-1)}{{x}^{5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3{x}^{2}}{4}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{3x-3}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}+(-\frac{3}{x}+\frac{3}{2{x}^{2}}){|}_{1}^{\infty } \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+3-\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

[:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152032 :question/worked-solution "The standard basis of $\text{M}_{n\times m}(\mathbb{R})$ contains a total of $n\cdot m$ matrices, each with one nonzero entry that is equal to $1.$ 

For example, the standard basis of $\text{M}_{3\times 2} (\mathbb{R})$ contains $3\cdot 2= 6$ elements, and is given by

![](images/8a/8a50f2d0ea7a7d24ca498b7e326bd66fb9afcfc089159146f07018c96fecfaf8.svg)

However, we're asked to find the dimension of $\text{M}_{5\times6}(\mathbb{R}),$ not $\text{M}_{3\times 2} (\mathbb{R}).$

If we were to repeat the same process above for the vector space $\text{M}_{5\times6}(\mathbb{R}),$ we would have $30$ matrices in our basis, meaning that

$$
\textrm{dim}(\text{M}_{5\times 6}(\mathbb{R})) = 5\cdot 6 =30.
$$

In general, 

$$
\textrm{dim}(\text{M}_{n\times m}(\mathbb{R})) = n\cdot m.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152220 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fa7720d1-24b7-56bb-ae25-fc2830d10498" "question-ec7f0e0d-aeea-55dc-8d79-107780421320" "question-c2dac37f-1586-5572-8aef-afd7b8fea459"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152030 :question/problem "Which of the following vector spaces has a dimension of $9?$

I. $\mathbb{R}^8$

II. $\mathbb{R}_8[t]$, the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $8$

III. $\text{M}_{3}(\mathbb{R}),$ the vector space of all $3 \times 3$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the vector spaces in turn.

I. Recall that $\textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n)=n.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^8)=8\neq 9.\quad {\color{red}{\times}}
  $$

II. Recall that $\textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}_{n}[t])=n+1.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}_{8}[t])=8+1=9.\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
  $$

III. Recall that $\textrm{dim}(\text{M}_{n}(\mathbb{R}))=n^2.$ Therefore, 

  $$
  \text{dim}(\text{M}_{3}(\mathbb{R}))=3^2=9.\quad {\color{green}{\checkmark}}
  $$

Hence, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152221 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a563102c-022c-5259-8c2a-2cd56b2b3d49" "question-133975da-da96-5b76-a610-069fd7ba3c88" "question-cf79cbf5-5d8d-5861-a04b-30929c364cf0"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152031 :question/problem "Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?

II. $\text{M}_{50\times100}(\mathbb{R}),$ the vector space of all $50 \times 100$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}$

III. $\mathbb{R}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomial functions in the variable $t$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186243971 :question/worked-solution "The standard basis of ${R}_{n}[t]$ is

$$

$$

$$

In general,

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{n}[t])=n+1.

$$
\{1, \: t, \: t^2\}.
$$

Another basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ is

$$
\big\{ t^2-1, \: t+3, \: 2t-1 \big\}.
$$

In general, vector spaces have infinitely many bases. 

Let's now consider the following theorem:

*If a basis of a vector space $V$ has $n$ elements, then every basis of $V$ has $n$ elements.*

The number $n$ is called the **dimension** of the vector space, and we write $\textrm{dim}(V)=n.$

So, since the standard basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ has $3$ elements, all of its bases have $3$ elements, and we write

$$
\textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}_2[t])=3.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186152367 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153161 :step/math-academy-id 653421 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153162 :step/math-academy-id 653422 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153166 :step/math-academy-id 653425 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153163 :step/math-academy-id 653428 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153164 :step/math-academy-id 653431 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186153165 :step/math-academy-id 653432 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100928 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-13bb3627-c113-57d8-978e-74ea6f5a6bbf"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100937 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e693a7c4-bdf1-528d-bafe-2fceb638714f" "question-81e7b982-4159-5f62-b6d4-f4e6663e3a07"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-13bb3627-c113-57d8-978e-74ea6f5a6bbf" :question/id #uuid "13bb3627-c113-57d8-978e-74ea6f5a6bbf" :question/math-academy-id "q-351919" :question/problem "Find the second-degree Taylor polynomial ${P}_{2}(x)$ of $f(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ about $x=\frac{\pi }{3}.$

${P}_{2}(x)=$
{{field-1}}$\,+$
{{field-2}}$(x-\frac{\pi }{3})\,-$
{{field-3}}${(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2}$" :question/worked-solution "To find the second-degree Taylor polynomial about $x=\frac{\pi }{3},$ we plug $a=\frac{\pi }{3}$ into the general formula to give

$$
{P}_{2}(x)=f(\frac{\pi }{3})+{f}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{3})(x-\frac{\pi }{3})+\frac{1}{2}{f}^{″}(\frac{\pi }{3}){(x-\frac{\pi }{3})}^{2}.
$$

$$

"b49a66f8-383d-5ed3-a1a9-b2f05fd8c09d" :question/math-academy-id "q-343873" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}-16y=f(x),$ where $$" :question/worked-solution "We assume that a solution of our equation has the following Fourier series:

$$
{y}_{p}∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}).

Now, we compute the derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}) \\ {y}_{p}^{″} & ∼\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{n\pi }{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2}))∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }-{a}_{n}\frac{{n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{n\pi x}{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the expressions for ${y}_{p}^{″}$ and ${y}_{p}$ into the equation and have

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe77b4de-90c9-5d84-bcb6-651adb4b6345"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fe77b4de-90c9-5d84-bcb6-651adb4b6345" :answer-field/id #uuid "fe77b4de-90c9-5d84-bcb6-651adb4b6345" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/select :answer-field/correct "answer-2cf7e913-fe58-5754-9149-b09245f9b60a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b701f81d-8ac2-5b72-b41d-29bb579466f5" "answer-2cf7e913-fe58-5754-9149-b09245f9b60a" "answer-6175ce1f-2050-5a57-bf7b-da70f7498dcd" "answer-53e18eaf-8bd1-5628-92d7-801bfaf1946a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b701f81d-8ac2-5b72-b41d-29bb579466f5" :answer/id #uuid "b701f81d-8ac2-5b72-b41d-29bb579466f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{n({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2cf7e913-fe58-5754-9149-b09245f9b60a" :answer/id #uuid "2cf7e913-fe58-5754-9149-b09245f9b60a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{16}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6175ce1f-2050-5a57-bf7b-da70f7498dcd" :answer/id #uuid "6175ce1f-2050-5a57-bf7b-da70f7498dcd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{4}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-53e18eaf-8bd1-5628-92d7-801bfaf1946a" :answer/id #uuid "53e18eaf-8bd1-5628-92d7-801bfaf1946a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{16}{{n}^{2}({n}^{2}{\pi }^{2}+64)}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-88bf7711-bb0b-51a9-9d4e-44874b161912" :question/id #uuid "88bf7711-bb0b-51a9-9d4e-44874b161912" :question/math-academy-id "q-343878" :question/problem "Select the missing parts in a particular solution of the differential equation ${y}^{″}+36y=f(x),$ where the Fourier series of the $6$-periodic forcing function is given by

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186397690 :question/worked-solution "We begin by identifying resonance. The differential equation

has a natural frequency of

For $n=3$, we have ${\omega }_{3}=6\pi .$ Since ${\omega }_{3}=\omega ,$ the $n=3$ harmonic of the forcing function causes resonance.

10\,?$

III. $x=5$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute each value into the given inequality and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}0}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <10 \\ 2\cdot x & <10 \\ 2\cdot 0 & <10 \\ 0 & <10\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=0$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $x=0$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}2}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <10 \\ 2\cdot x & <10 \\ 2\cdot 2 & <10 \\ 4 & <10\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=2$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $x=2$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}5}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <10 \\ 2\cdot x & <10 \\ 2\cdot 5 & <10 \\ 10 & <10\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=5$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $x=5$ **does not satisfy** this inequality." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068785 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-44ec8528-0626-53ff-b6b0-f0595765d80d" "question-7ec4ef84-8b35-542a-b22f-98607c9a4fdd"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068627 :question/problem "Which of the following values of $t$ satisfy the inequality $\dfrac{2t}{3} < 8\,?$

I. $t=9$

II. $t=6$

III. $t=3$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute each value into the given inequality and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}t}={\color{blue}9}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot 9}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{18}{3} & <8 \\ 6 & <8\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $t = 9$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $t=9$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}t}={\color{blue}6}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot 6}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{12}{3} & <8 \\ 4 & <8\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $t=6$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $t=6$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}t}={\color{blue}3}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot t}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{2\cdot 3}{3} & <8 \\ \frac{6}{3} & <8 \\ 2 & <8\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $t=3$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $t=3$ **satisfies** this inequality." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068783 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-54c177e7-bfd3-5330-bd52-c67fa05a6194"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068625 :question/problem "Which of the following values of $x$ satisfy the inequality $1 \leq \dfrac{x}{2}-1 < 3\,?$

I. $x=0$

II. $x=4$

III. $x=10$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute each value into the given inequality and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}0}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \le \frac{x}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le \frac{0}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le 0-1<3 \\ 1 & \le -1<3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=0$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $x=0$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}4}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \le \frac{x}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le \frac{4}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le 2-1<3 \\ 1 & \le 1<3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=4$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $x=4$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}x}={\color{blue}10}$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \le \frac{x}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le \frac{10}{2}-1<3 \\ 1 & \le 5-1<3 \\ 1 & \le 4<3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=10$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $x=10$ **does not satisfy** this inequality." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068784 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cad781ca-8e12-5b8d-a5a5-787d8ffa6e99" "question-516935e4-c5da-561b-9d27-f7806d4435cd" "question-ed3aeee5-2189-5d52-8e31-431c161f29f9" "question-b784d723-3b79-553d-9de5-8ee50049511b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068626 :question/problem "The value $a = 2$ satisfies which of the following inequalities?

I. $\dfrac{a}{2} + 2 > 5$

II. $1 \leq 2a < 6$

III. $3a - 1 < 10$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute the given value into each of the inequalities and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}2}$ into the first inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a}{2}+2 & >5 \\ \frac{2}{2}+2 & >5 \\ 1+2 & >5 \\ 3 & >5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $a = 2$ leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $a = 2$ ** does not satisfy** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}a}={\color{blue}2}$ into the second inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & \le 2a<6 \\ 1 & \le 2\cdot a<6 \\ 1 & \le 2\cdot 2<6 \\ 1 & \le 4<6\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $a = 2$ leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $a = 2$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value ${\color{blue}a} = {\color{blue}2}$ into the third inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}3a-1 & <10 \\ 3\cdot a-1 & <10 \\ 3\cdot 2-1 & <10 \\ 5 & <10\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $a = 2$ leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $a = 2$ **satisfies** this inequality." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-78ade5bf-b2b7-57c1-a1d4-ab36482d20cd" :question/id #uuid "78ade5bf-b2b7-57c1-a1d4-ab36482d20cd" :question/math-academy-id "q-63544" :question/problem "Which of the following values of $v$ satisfy the inequality $7v\le 28\,?$

II. $2x\le 10$

III. $1<x+5<6$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute the given value into each of the inequalities and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

$$

$$

Therefore, $x=4$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value $x=4$ into the third inequality. We get:

$$

For example, which of the following values of $y$ satisfy the inequality $y - 1 > 3\,?$

I. $y=6$

II. $y=2$

III. $y=3$

Let's go through the possibilities one at a time.

- Substituting the value ${\color{blue}y}={\color{blue}6}$ into the given equation, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & >3 \\ 6-1 & >3 \\ 5 & >3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This is a **true** statement, so $y=6$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- Substituting the value ${\color{blue}y}={\color{blue}2}$ into the given equation, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & >3 \\ 2-1 & >3 \\ 1 & >3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

This is a **false** statement, so $y=2$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

- Substituting the value ${\color{blue}y}={\color{blue}3}$ into the given equation, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & >3 \\ 3-1 & >3 \\ 2 & >3\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

This is a **false** statement, so $y=3$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

Therefore, only I satisfies the inequality." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068934 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186120545 :question/answer-fields 17592186119383] {:db/id 17592186119874 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-988956df-fafe-5af5-9e6f-367acfc61887"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-988956df-fafe-5af5-9e6f-367acfc61887" :question/id #uuid "988956df-fafe-5af5-9e6f-367acfc61887" :question/math-academy-id "q-42570" :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
det(H)=det[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 6 \\ 3 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot det[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 3 \\ -3 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
