**Step 1.**  We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix. Since matrix $A$ is triangular, its eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal: 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=-3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-2$

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-3)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $2$nd one). Thus, ${x}_{1}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a homogeneous system of linear equations with the matrix as above. Note, the matrix is already in row echelon form. There is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "260bb0c0-f4cc-5171-8f8e-251abb929092" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436963}} {:db/id 17592186436963 :step/content {:db/id 17592186404114 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "20692b0c-ecf3-5857-b371-5e00dd088456" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 3.** We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the invertible matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c086434a-2e61-5437-a45d-1dd3277fb4b0"} {:db/id 17592186436964 :step/content {:db/id 17592186348376 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5b5beb30-0a75-5fc1-9136-9135683b1b51" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346129} {:answer/id #uuid "70a5b71d-efb0-58ab-af42-12eed66f2bb6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346339} {:answer/id #uuid "783aadac-abc2-5341-8883-bae757b2fee4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & -11\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346406} {:answer/id #uuid "78aeeb6e-6d38-58dc-93e3-4da1e56572c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186346408} {:answer/id #uuid "df14a525-a2b3-5a1d-8fb5-695c415e41e5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]$ and $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]$" :db/id 17592186347312}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186347312} :answer-field/id #uuid "feb4a3c4-e3c2-59e1-b4f8-a58de2ef0e9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186348050}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e9500f77-53af-537c-9030-31932253fda8" :question/math-academy-id "q-80372" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ -4 & -6\end{aligned}].$ You're given that ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, and

**Step 1.** We need to find the eigenvalues of the matrix $B$ using its characteristic equation $det(B-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-5-\lambda  & 3 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-5-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-3\cdot (-6) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda -2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, the eigenvalues of $B$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ 

**Step 2.** Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $B.$

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}B-I & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 3 \\ -6 & 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to its row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$  Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=2,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ -6 & 6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & ={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$
is diagonalizable or not, and if it is diagonalizable, find a corresponding diagonal matrix $D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is triangular, the eigenvalues are the entries on the main diagonal. 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix $(A-4I)\text{x}=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 8 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has only $1$ pivot column. This implies that we will have only $2-1=1$ linearly independent eigenvector corresponding to the current eigenvalue. Therefore, $A$ is not diagonalizable."} :step/id #uuid "f50c4f35-60de-5348-bbfd-204a572ac060" :step/next {:db/id 17592186436964}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "The unit tangent vector to a curve at an arbitrary point is given by

$$
T(t)=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t).
$$

Find the principal normal vector at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ if 

$$
\begin{aligned}q(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨3,0,-4⟩,\,{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})=⟨0,3,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5})\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{5}\cdot q(t)+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{5}\cdot q(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})}{5}\cdot {q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{q}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨0,3,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖ & =\frac{3}{5}\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})}{‖{T}^{′}(\frac{\pi }{2})‖} \\  & =\frac{\frac{3}{5}⟨0,1,0⟩}{(\frac{3}{5})} \\  & =⟨0,1,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot N(\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\frac{1}{5}q(\frac{\pi }{2})\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨3,0,-4⟩\cdot ⟨0,1,0⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\cdot 0+0\cdot 1-4\cdot 0) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186398312 :question/id #uuid "d020d9fa-ec2e-5a71-a105-bba07f29c4ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-127583"} {:db/id 17592186398319 :question/id #uuid $$

$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we calculate ${T}^{′}(t)$ and evaluate it at $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot q(t)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2})\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(q(t)) \\  & =-\frac{2t}{({t}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(t)+\frac{1}{{t}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(t) \\  \\ {T}^{′}(0) & =-\frac{2(0)}{({0}^{2}+2)^{2}}\cdot q(0)+\frac{1}{{0}^{2}+2}\cdot {q}^{′}(0) \\  & =0(\sqrt{2}\,i+j+k)+\frac{1}{2}(-2\,j+2\,k) \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Next, we find the magnitude of ${T}^{′}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{T}^{′}(0)‖ & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize ${T}^{′}(0)$ and obtain the principal normal to the curve at the point where $t=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}N(0) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(0)}{‖{T}^{′}(0)‖} \\  & =\frac{-j+k}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-j+k)\end{aligned}
$$

Note that when we find the scalar product of $T$ and $N$ at the point where $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}T(0)\cdot N(0) & =\frac{1}{2}q(0)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-j+k) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{2}\,i+j+k)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-j+k) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(-j\cdot j+k\cdot k) \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}(-1+1) \\  & =0.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186442608 :question/id #uuid "35b2b5dc-be5b-531e-92b7-e1931e890d8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-127596"} {:db/id 17592186442611 :question/id #uuid "aef82e82-0717-5dbd-b71e-34fa8441f954" :topic/math-academy-id 1795} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that 

- is perpendicular to the unit tangent vector, and

- points in the direction that the curve is bending.

In general, if the unit tangent vector is given by $\mathbf T(t),$ then the principal normal vector is given by

$$
\mathbf N(t)= \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{\|\mathbf T'(t)\|},
$$

where it is assumed that $\|\mathbf T'(t)\|\neq 0.$

To demonstrate, suppose that the curve $C$ is parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf f(t) = \left\langle 2\cos t, \: 2\sin t \right\rangle, \qquad t \in [0, \pi].
$$

We will compute the principal normal vector at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4}.$

First, using the formula for the unit tangent, $\mathbf T(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf f'(t)}{||\mathbf f'(t)||},$ we find that the general unit tangent vector is

$$
\mathbf T(t)= \left\langle {-\sin t}, \cos t\right\rangle.
$$

Now, when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},$ we have the point $P(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).$ The unit tangent vector $\mathbf{T}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ and the principal normal vector $\mathbf{N}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)$ at this point are shown below:

![](images/d0/d0a30a44bb825a8a12ca54153b6223b9bf0c2b754245b21650a5664db5e1647e.png)

To calculate the principal normal vector, we start by calculating the derivative of the unit tangent function. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩ \\ {T}^{′}(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general principal normal vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{||{T}^{′}(t)||} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩}{\sqrt{1}} \\  & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find $\mathbf N\left(\dfrac\pi 4\right),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(\frac{\pi }{4}) & =⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}),\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2},-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, it's easy to check that $\mathbf T'(t)$ and $\mathbf N'(t)$ are perpendicular for all $t$ by computing the dot product and showing that we get zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t)\cdot N(t) & =⟨-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\cdot ⟨-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,-\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0\,✓\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "03709847-4a63-5975-b20a-1d6693ceadb3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9376 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "c3443d00-c515-5a63-93a0-747d76d2271c" :step/math-academy-id 626149 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120642}} {:db/id 17592186120642 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119785 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119532 :question/id #uuid "8cb590c5-586d-56a1-af70-d693ea055419" :question/math-academy-id "e-14996"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "930466fc-c7fe-51a5-8634-818abddd0da9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050685}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120242} {:db/id 17592186120252} {:db/id 17592186262761} {:db/id 17592186311553} {:db/id 17592186344986} {:db/id 17592186398305} {:db/id 17592186442610} {:db/id 17592186442613}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at a Given Point"} :step/id #uuid "c9c3f801-f35a-5089-8d66-01d0fd9903d2" :step/math-academy-id 626150 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120643}} {:db/id 17592186120643 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119786 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119533 :question/id #uuid "2f92f568-0bf5-58bd-87ce-e6be8d05fe69" :question/math-academy-id "e-14997"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8d21e1c3-1529-5471-a1e6-76f174da79c3" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120163} {:db/id 17592186120164} {:db/id 17592186290398} {:db/id 17592186290399} {:db/id 17592186290400} {:db/id 17592186290401} {:db/id 17592186290402} {:db/id 17592186323724} {:db/id 17592186323725} {:db/id 17592186442609} {:db/id 17592186442614}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Principal Normal at an Arbitrary Point"} :step/id #uuid "812571c6-b194-5ab1-b16a-bcf2ac6ffbe9" :step/math-academy-id 626153 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120644}} {:db/id 17592186120644 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121149 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf T(t)$ be the unit tangent vector to some differentiable vector-valued function. Since $||\mathbf T(t)|| = 1,$ and $\mathbf T(t)$ is obviously parallel to itself, we must have

$$
\mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) = 1.
$$

Differentiating the above relationship with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\mathbf T'(t) \cdot \mathbf T(t) + \mathbf T(t) \cdot \mathbf T'(t) = 0,
$$

which can be simplified as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t)+{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ 2{T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0 \\ {T}^{′}(t)\cdot T(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, provided that $\mathbf T'(t)\neq \mathbf 0,$ then it must be the case that $\mathbf T'(t)$ is perpendicular to $\mathbf T(t).$

The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures the rate of change of $\mathbf T(t).$ However, since $\mathbf T(t)$ is a unit vector for all $t,$ it changes only in its direction. The vector $\mathbf T'(t)$ measures this rate of change in direction. 

To form the principal normal $\mathbf N(t),$ we normalize $\mathbf T'(t),$ which leads to the definition

$$
\mathbf N(t) = \dfrac{\mathbf T'(t)}{||\mathbf T'(t)||}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "bd9190b9-f59c-5c06-987a-c6269ec9b3a7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9377 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula for the Principal Normal"} :step/id #uuid "ee849a7a-e449-5317-872e-183c46fabb72" :step/math-academy-id 626156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120645}} {:db/id 17592186120645 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119787 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119534 :question/id #uuid "f5e6498b-73f9-5760-81bb-14e9acc495f8" :question/math-academy-id "e-14998"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "01fe665f-05e8-5183-9c98-cb760af0ae02" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120520} {:db/id 17592186120521} {:db/id 17592186262795} {:db/id 17592186262799} {:db/id 17592186345083} {:db/id 17592186345091} {:db/id 17592186398312} {:db/id 17592186398319} {:db/id 17592186398326} {:db/id 17592186442608} {:db/id 17592186442611} {:db/id 17592186442612}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Principal Normal Given Some Information About a Curve"} :step/id #uuid "8e583ccb-952c-52c6-b8a9-e4b716f0d3c4" :step/math-academy-id 626157 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120646}} {:db/id 17592186120646 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121150 :tutorial/content "Consider the straight line given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

 

If we attempt to calculate its principal normal vector, we will get an interesting result. First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|
\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\begin{aligned}-2+5t \\ 1 \\ \sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the case of a straight line, $\mathbf T(t)$ is simply the (normalized) direction vector, as we would expect. 

Next, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}]=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is the zero vector, we can't normalize it as usual. If we try to apply the usual formula we get an undefined result due to division by zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{0}{‖0‖}=\frac{0}{0}=\text{undefined}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a straight line does not have a principal normal.

The intuition behind this result is that the principal normal points in the direction in which a curve is bending, but a straight line does not bend at all." :tutorial/id #uuid "5c27df4b-0d17-5407-997b-c240d492eeca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9378 :tutorial/title "Lines Do Not Have Principal Normal Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "1aa2d247-5dd4-5fdf-a44a-9cf0a8cd1e0d" :step/math-academy-id 626160}] :activity/title "Principal Normal Vectors" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186120013} {:db/id 17592186120641 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121148 :tutorial/content "The **principal normal vector** to a curve $C$ at a point $P$ is a unit vector that

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+t\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

 

If we attempt to calculate its principal normal vector, we will get an interesting result. First, we calculate $\mathbf r'(t)$ and $\|\mathbf r'(t)\|
\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[\begin{aligned}-2+5t \\ 1 \\ \sqrt{2}t\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the unit tangent vector is

$$
\begin{aligned}T(t) & =\frac{{r}^{′}(t)}{‖{r}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0 \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in the case of a straight line, $\mathbf T(t)$ is simply the (normalized) direction vector, as we would expect. 

Next, we calculate $\mathbf T'(t)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{′}(t) & =\frac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\,[\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(0) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2})\end{aligned}]=0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{T}'(t)$ is the zero vector, we can't normalize it as usual. If we try to apply the usual formula we get an undefined result due to division by zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}N(t) & =\frac{{T}^{′}(t)}{‖{T}^{′}(t)‖}=\frac{0}{‖0‖}=\frac{0}{0}=\text{undefined}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a straight line does not have a principal normal.

The intuition behind this result is that the principal normal points in the direction in which a curve is bending, but a straight line does not bend at all." :tutorial/id #uuid "5c27df4b-0d17-5407-997b-c240d492eeca" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9378 :tutorial/title "Lines Do Not Have Principal Normal Vectors"} :step/id #uuid "1aa2d247-5dd4-5fdf-a44a-9cf0a8cd1e0d" :step/math-academy-id 626160} {:db/id 17592186121150 :tutorial/content "Consider the straight line given by

:knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Generated by the Square of a Sum"}] :question/problem "Factor $9x^2+30x+25$." :question/worked-solution "The "square of a sum" formula states that

$$
a^2 + {\color{red}{2}}a{\color{blue}{b}} + {\color{blue}b}^2 = (a+{\color{blue}{b}})^2
$$

We will use this formula to factor the given trinomial. Our trinomial is

$$
9x^2+30x+25
$$

First, we write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

$$
(3x)^{2} + 30x + (5)^{2}
$$

Next, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:
$(3x)^{2} + 2(15x) + (5)^{2}$

Then, we write the middle parentheses $(15x)$ as a product of $3x$ and ${\color{blue}5}$:
$(3x)^{2} + 2(3x \cdot 5) + (5)^{2}$

Finally, we factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula with $a=3x$ and

$$
{\color{blue}{b}} = {\color{blue}{5}}
$$

This gives
$(3x + 5)^{2}$"} {:db/id 17592186049026} {:db/id 17592186069216 :question/id #uuid "c7e16146-85d4-59f8-9f0f-78b375bf7200" :question/math-academy-id "q-3005"} {:db/id 17592186069252 :question/id #uuid "6d26bd33-b4df-5fea-8716-a151a462b4de" :question/math-academy-id "q-31970"} {:db/id 17592186068848 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068465 :question/id #uuid "e9c8bdc9-696d-5a55-bb0d-d247008c5684" :question/math-academy-id "e-1333"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f64efad-73ef-5caa-b38b-060d24ce13cf" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069219 :question/id #uuid "d1802f9f-ebf2-5470-b37a-d4a94669b876" :question/math-academy-id "q-3008"} {:db/id 17592186069220 :question/id #uuid "11047f98-24ac-5e85-994b-d2cd73e1984b" :question/math-academy-id "q-3009"}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Whose Terms Have a Common Factor"} {:db/id 17592186068465 :question/id #uuid "e9c8bdc9-696d-5a55-bb0d-d247008c5684" :question/math-academy-id "e-1333" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186068848 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f64efad-73ef-5caa-b38b-060d24ce13cf" :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Whose Terms Have a Common Factor"}] :question/problem "Factor the expression $7a^2+28a+28$." :question/worked-solution "Before we start our normal process of factoring, notice that all of the terms have a common factor of $7$. Therefore, we can simplify the expression by factoring out $7$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
7a^{2} + 28a + 28 &=  \\
&= 7(a^{2} + 4a + 4)
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's factor the expression inside parentheses using the square of sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} + 4a + 4 &=  \\
&= a^{2} + 4a + 2^{2} \\
&= a^{2} + 2 \cdot 2a + 2^{2} \\
&= (a + 2)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
7(a^{2} + 4a + 4) &=  \\
&= 7(a + 2)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186069219 :question/id #uuid "d1802f9f-ebf2-5470-b37a-d4a94669b876" :question/math-academy-id "q-3008"} {:db/id 17592186069220 :question/id #uuid "Factor $-16y^2 + 4y - \dfrac{1}{4}$." :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is negative. To reduce the expression to a more familiar form, we can factor out $-1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-16y^{2} + 4y - \frac{1}{4} &=  \\
&= - (16y^{2} - 4y + \frac{1}{4})
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the quadratic expression inside the parentheses using the sum of difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
16y^{2} - 4y + \frac{1}{4} &=  \\
(4y)^{2} - 4y + (\frac{1}{2})^{2} &=  \\
(4y)^{2} - 2 \cdot (2y) + (\frac{1}{2})^{2} &=  \\
(4y)^{2} - 2 \cdot (4y \cdot \frac{1}{2}) + (\frac{1}{2})^{2} &=  \\
&= (4y - \frac{1}{2})^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
- (16y^{2} - 4y + \frac{1}{4}) &=  \\
&= - (4y - \frac{1}{2})^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186069338 :question/id #uuid "c9fa9a0f-8fe4-5c82-84dd-1780d298cb84" :question/math-academy-id "q-44095"} {:db/id 17592186069339 :question/id #uuid "7f41180f-6973-5abe-bb70-62dea9df68d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-44096"} {:db/id 17592186068902 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068520 :question/id #uuid "b7141e58-61cf-5134-8443-a82d79a5506e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1593"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "69a3b7a7-1042-511a-aaff-8b0911eae499" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069215 :question/id #uuid "62c062a9-da9c-5b27-a479-ed76519df49f" :question/math-academy-id "q-3004"} {:db/id 17592186069251 :question/id #uuid "7bde15d7-a93b-50f3-9b14-a29e7dbd01c9" :question/math-academy-id "q-31969"}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Generated by the Square of a Difference"} {:db/id 17592186068520 :question/id #uuid "b7141e58-61cf-5134-8443-a82d79a5506e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1593" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186068902 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "69a3b7a7-1042-511a-aaff-8b0911eae499" :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Generated by the Square of a Difference"}] :question/problem "Factor $9y^2-12y+4$." :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$

$$

$$

$(3y)^{2} - 12y + (2)^{2}$

Next, we factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

For example, the expression

$$
4x^2+12x+9
$$

has a leading coefficient of $4$, and it is a perfect square trinomial because it is the square of the binomial $(2x+3)$ as we can see below:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(2x + 3)^{2} &=  \\
(2x)^{2} + 2(2x)(3) + (3)^{2} &=  \\
&= 4x^{2} + 12x + 9
\end{aligned}
$$

To factor a perfect square trinomial with a leading coefficient other than $1$, we use the square of sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{2} + 2ab + b^{2} &= (a + b)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $4x^2+12x+9$ using the square of sum formula. We perform the following steps:

1. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:
$4x^{2} + 12x + 9|=; (2x)^{2} + 12x + (3)^{2}$
2. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:
$(2x)^{2} + 2(6x) + (3)^{2}$
3. Write the middle parentheses $(6x)$ as a product of $2x$ and ${\color{blue}3}$:
$(2x)^{2} + 2(2x \cdot 3) + (3)^{2}$
4. Factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula. In this case, we have $a=2x$ and $b=3$:
$(2x + 3)^{2}$

**Note:** This method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial. $-(25y^2 - 20y + 4)$

Now, we factor the quadratic expression inside the parentheses using the square of a difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
25y^{2} - 20y + 4 &=  \\
(5y)^{2} - 20y + 2^{2} &=  \\
(5y)^{2} - 2(10y) + 2^{2} &=  \\
(5y)^{2} - 2(5y \cdot 2) + 2^{2} &=  \\
&= (5y - 2)^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
- (25y^{2} - 20y + 4) &=  \\
&= - (5y - 2)^{2}
\end{aligned}

1" :db/id 17592186067737} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186069797} :activity/id #uuid "f64241dc-95fe-569e-8afc-913a546e0d46" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048170 :topic/id #uuid "8555552a-fb5f-5455-9150-c473e5580702" :topic/math-academy-id 381} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069719 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068796 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068639 :question/id #uuid "ca60143b-d02c-5497-a134-56444304c2fa" :question/math-academy-id "e-7223"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3979b4ea-910f-5037-b8e8-b0297f31c47c" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069425} {:db/id 17592186069427}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Cube Roots of Terms Containing Binomials"} :step/id #uuid "20d6dd44-7fc6-52a1-a076-27ddb6da9696" :step/math-academy-id 26723 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069799}} {:db/id 17592186069797 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069942 :tutorial/content "To find the **cube root** of a number $x$, we must ask ourselves, "what number *cubed* equals $x$?"

For example, the cube root of $8$ is $2$ since

$$
2^3 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8
$$

and the cube root of $-8$ is $-2$ since

$$
(-2)^3 = (-2) \cdot (-2) \cdot (-2) = -8
$$

In general, the cube root of $x^3$ is $x$.

Like the square root, the cube root is signified by a radical symbol, but it also has a little $3$ next to it, i.e., $\sqrt[3\!\phantom{p}]{\phantom{2}}$. Using this notation, we can express the above statements mathematically:

- "The cube root of $8$ is $2$" can be expressed as $\sqrt[3]{8}=2$.
- "The cube root of $-8$ is $-2$" can be expressed as $\sqrt[3]{-8}=-2$.
- "The cube root of $x^3$ is $x$" can be expressed as $\sqrt[3]{x^3}=x$.

**Note:** For square roots, we have

$$
\sqrt{x^2} = \mid x \mid
$$

but for cube roots, we have

$$
\sqrt[3]{x^3} = x
$$

No absolute value is needed for cube roots, because

- the cube root of a positive number is a positive number, and
- the cube root of a negative number is a negative number." :tutorial/id #uuid "ad1bc727-9054-5115-83f0-a82aa24dc35e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1605 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7e24a880-f9da-5e1e-b0bf-5bb2128d72a1" :step/math-academy-id 4295 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069798}} {:db/id 17592186069798 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068850 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068467 :question/id #uuid "2ca53a08-7b11-552c-983f-96e7a392156c" :question/math-academy-id "e-1357"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "942732a6-ca14-5b61-b8fb-ab9ef81610cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049843}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069210} {:db/id 17592186069418}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Cube Root of a Monomial"} :step/id #uuid "eea06921-8121-51a7-86ad-15824cc00550" :step/math-academy-id 4296 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069719}} {:db/id 17592186069799 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068851 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068468 :question/id #uuid "c52719a7-544b-5844-b716-9b9d2999c028" :question/math-academy-id "e-1358"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "11c07788-b01d-5788-b2f1-0a027ea53cb2" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069424} {:db/id 17592186069426}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Cube Root of a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "f7015e37-4cd2-5ffb-814e-264ca9a0b345" :step/math-academy-id 4299}] :activity/title "The Cube Root of a Perfect Cube With Algebraic Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186068929} {:db/id 17592186069797 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069942 :tutorial/content "To find the **cube root** of a number $x$, we must ask ourselves, "what number *cubed* equals $x$?"

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$" :question/worked-solution "Substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{24}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{24}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{6} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4{z}^{2} & =24 \\ (4t)^{2}+(8t)^{2}+4(2t)^{2} & =24 \\ 16{t}^{2}+64{t}^{2}+16{t}^{2} & =24 \\ 96{t}^{2} & =24 \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solution $t = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}.$ 

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-\dfrac 1 2,$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4(-\frac{1}{2})=-2 \\ y=8(-\frac{1}{2})=-4 \\ z=2(-\frac{1}{2})=-1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $\left(-2,-4,-1\right).$

- For $t=\dfrac 1 2,$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=4(\frac{1}{2})=2 \\ y=8(\frac{1}{2})=4 \\ z=2(\frac{1}{2})=1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $\left(2,4,1\right).$

between the ellipsoid $\dfrac{(x+1)^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}+\dfrac{z^2}{16}=1$ and the plane $x-z=3$ onto the $yz$-plane." :question/worked-solution "Since we want to find the projection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x.$ First, we solve for $x$ in the equation of the plane, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-z=3\,⟹\,x=z+3\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the expression for $x$ into the equation of the ellipsoid, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{((z+3)+1)^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{(z+4)^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{z}^{2}+8z+16}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{2{z}^{2}+8z+16}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}+4z+8}{8} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, by completing the square for the variable $z,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{z}^{2}+4z+8}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{({z}^{2}+4z+4)+4}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(z+2)^{2}+4}{8} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(z+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{1}{2} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{4}+\frac{(z+2)^{2}}{8} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{(z+2)^{2}}{4} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the projection of the intersection is the ellipse $\dfrac{y^2}{2}+\dfrac{(z+2)^2}{4} = 1.$"} {:db/id 17592186198995 :question/id #uuid "0f6c4178-bc50-541f-bab7-025040917393" elliptic cone $x^2 + y^2=z^2$ and the line $x +1=y-1 =\dfrac{z}{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:
![](images/41/41e6a96cc57d9ce57d5a7bec35586175d9217f92e4dc2bab106db641db9f24ea.png)
where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Substituting the above expressions for $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ into the equation of the elliptic cone, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ (t-1)^{2}+(t+1)^{2} & =(2t)^{2} \\ {t}^{2}-2t+1+{t}^{2}+2t+1 & =4{t}^{2} \\ 2{t}^{2}+2 & =4{t}^{2} \\ 2 & =2{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =1 \\ t & =\pm 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute our solutions back into the equations of the line.

- For $t=-1,$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1-1=-2 \\ y=-1+1=0 \\ z=2(-1)=-2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $\left(-2,0,-2\right).$

- For $t=1,$ we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1-1=0 \\ y=1+1=2 \\ z=2(1)=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $\left(0,2,2\right).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(-2,0,-2)$ and $(0,2,2).$"} {:db/id 17592186198994 :question/id #uuid "3624fa42-c59d-5231-bc08-94f56f4ab26d" :question/math-academy-id "q-70570" intersection of the elliptic paraboloid 
$z=x^2+y^2$
and the plane 
$z = x+y-\dfrac{1}{4},$
as shown below.

![](images/1d/1d4b8db0985d437807f6e580bc6c2c16cacca1ea7c8e49ed4653717cdb3c9e27.png)

Note that the intersection of the paraboloid and plane is given by the solution to the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ z=x+y-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xy$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $z$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/52/520b57cf872ede31d4397d59a833c565147d82a45be1d6b2634f82e1effdff8c.png)

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $xz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $y$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/05/059acf1ec5dadaa98b2cd4d4b6c79884e4facc96dd49664abbc247cfba86aaeb.png)

- To find the projection of the intersection onto the $yz$-plane, we need to eliminate the variable $x$ from the system. The resulting projection curve will be an ellipse, as depicted below.

![](images/80/80d3042d21d2e7265a40739ae1531ac30b03fea16fa67609a4e1b0eac8559411.png)

Let's see some examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "1d0d1b4d-a008-573c-b368-9ab2bfc7f41c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7833 :tutorial/title "Intersections of Surfaces With Planes"} :step/id #uuid "d692d6c4-d307-5093-8885-932a55dd02f4" :step/math-academy-id 45271 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199240}} {:db/id 17592186199370 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199500 :tutorial/content "Suppose we wish to find the points of intersection of the elliptic paraboloid 
$z=x^2+y^2$
and the line with the equation
$x = -y = -z+1.$
The line, paraboloid, and their points of intersection are shown below.

![](images/51/5159ac99a1bc9f73c01df3c2cc2e6fb2093a3d68e00731609d7b62a6fa55149d.png)

The trick is to express the equation of the line in parametric form, substitute the parametric equations into the equation of the surface, and solve for the parameter.

So, first, we write the equation of our line in the parametric form:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=t \\ y=-t \\ z=-t+1\end{aligned}
$$

where $t \in (-\infty,\infty).$

Our intersection points must belong to the line and the surface simultaneously. So, substituting the expressions for $x$, $y$, and $z$ from the parametric equation of the line into the equation of the paraboloid, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ (-t+1) & =(t)^{2}+(-t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Simplifying this equation, we get

$$
2t^2+t - 1=0.
$$

The solutions to this equation are
$t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $t=-1.$ 

Substituting these values back into the parametric equations of the line

- For $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$, we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{1}{2} \\ y=-(\frac{1}{2})=-\frac{1}{2} \\ z=-(\frac{1}{2})+1=\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the first point is $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2}).$

- For $t=-1$, we have

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=(-1)=-1 \\ y=-(-1)=1 \\ z=-(-1)+1=2,\end{aligned}
$$

so the second point is $(-1,1,2).$

Therefore, the points of intersection are $(\dfrac{1}{2},-\dfrac{1}{2},\dfrac{1}{2})$ and $(-1,1,2).$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following determinants are equal to $0?$

$$
|A|=|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ \sqrt{5} & 0 & 4 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|B|=|\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}|,\,|C|=|\begin{aligned}4 & \sqrt{3} & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & \sqrt{5} & 1\end{aligned}|
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the given determinants in turn.

- The matrix $A$ has a zero column: 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 1 \\ \sqrt{5} & 0 & 4 \\ -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

As a result, $|A|=0.$

- Since $B$ is a diagonal matrix, we obtain 

$$
|B|=3\cdot (-1)\cdot 5=-15\ne 0.
$$

- The matrix $C$ has identical columns: 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & \sqrt{3} & 4 \\ 2 & 4 & 2 \\ 1 & \sqrt{5} & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

As a result, $|C|=0.$

$$
|A|=|\begin{aligned}\sqrt{3} & 5 & -1 \\ 4 & -3 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|B|=|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & -\sqrt{3} & 4\end{aligned}|,\,|C|=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & -1 \\ 6 & \sqrt{3} & 3 \\ -4 & \sqrt{7} & -2\end{aligned}|.

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ has two identical rows

- **II.** One of the rows/columns of $A$ is proportional to another row/column of $A$

- **III.** $A$ has two identical columns" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.

- Statements I and III are false. For example, consider the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}].
$$

We have that 

$$
|A|=1\cdot 8-4\cdot 2=0
$$

but $A$ has neither two identical rows nor two identical columns.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

In the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix, this means that one of the rows/columns must be proportional to another row/column.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} {:db/id 17592186272012 :question/id #uuid "f60fdb9d-cf89-59bd-ad65-e9ec096b82df" :question/math-academy-id "q-140049" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "643b4a3a-7263-51ad-8b17-fdd82678cf99" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186464084} {:answer/id #uuid "e3e66fb8-1a18-56f4-8033-3baba4940db9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186464085}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186464084} :answer-field/id #uuid "2ceb200f-e369-571b-b619-8f16a603488c" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186464976} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "198009c8-d9e6-556e-aa1c-228a37b12311" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186464086} {:answer/id #uuid "da19cf9c-0b56-5a20-b004-c70d313f5184" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186464087}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186464087} :answer-field/id #uuid "d98905ac-4493-5551-96b2-6d52f8e3f566" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186464977} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "63ea76cf-d936-573e-a0be-56de7954b8ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186464088} {:answer/id #uuid "24e2aa19-faca-5a81-a238-e9e984e89ef4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186464089}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186464089} :answer-field/id #uuid "ed42e6d2-1aff-5708-ad8c-b45de0195450" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186464978}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix such that $|A|\ne 0.$ Which of the following statements must be true?
- **I.** $A$ is a triangular matrix
- **II.** $A$ does not have identical rows
- **III.** $A$ does not have proportional columns

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. For example, consider the matrix 

$$

$$

We have that 

$$

$$

but $A$ is not a triangular matrix.

- Statements II and III are true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

In the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix, this means that one of the rows/columns must be proportional to another row/column.
Hence, if $|A|\ne 0$ then $A$ doesn't have proportional nor identical rows/columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only"."} {:db/id 17592186272013 :question/id #uuid "14e63fd3-62b7-575e-b489-4cda5c20ed53" :question/math-academy-id "q-140050" :knowledge-point/_questions - **III.** One of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-2)+(1-2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

but $A$ has neither a zero column nor two proportional rows.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

:topic/math-academy-id 2201} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135151 :tutorial/content "If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

For example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:

![](images/6b/6bb8b64f7ed8730e641cdf88fc6fe7add40bc15061095c6b1f57c1b764b28feb.svg)

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+2}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}|+(-1)^{2+3}(0)|\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{aligned}| \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero." :tutorial/id #uuid "cee0a552-60f2-5785-a506-63bd053364c7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6888 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b68428f5-f5bb-5090-b7f9-4971dc931914" :step/math-academy-id 41745 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134902}} {:db/id 17592186134902 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135152 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:

![](images/74/7477781b618ec384b1638d01707acf545e7d9882ffca5bbc0efde4e224b04308.svg)

We can subtract the $1$st row from the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "6813d49e-3908-5735-8196-8e1aad5a14e6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6889 :tutorial/title "Determinants with Identical Rows or Identical Columns"} :step/id #uuid "e105e6ae-64b8-5812-85e8-b5c3ef7b6c7d" :step/math-academy-id 41746 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134903}} {:db/id 17592186134903 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133911 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133466 :question/id #uuid "bb2795c3-6359-50d8-9531-1e9dfae7a2ce" :question/math-academy-id "e-10994"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "28142e26-f6c7-54c9-9c16-035c75f7659f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048462} {:db/id 17592186049159}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134395} {:db/id 17592186134408} {:db/id 17592186272009} {:db/id 17592186329700} {:db/id 17592186351408} {:db/id 17592186400867} {:db/id 17592186420351} {:db/id 17592186420352} {:db/id 17592186427636}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Determinant of a Matrix With A Zero Row/Column or Two Identical Rows/Columns"} :step/id #uuid "f2a27f52-c605-5d01-84c1-49531f59d922" :step/math-academy-id 41747 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134904}} {:db/id 17592186134904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135153 :tutorial/content "Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows and no identical rows but it has two proportional rows:

![](images/81/8181d36ff1378310744b0d74f42f2934eb1e41053f45ecfeacf0c813abe994df.svg)

We can add three times the $1$st row to the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -3 & -6 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two proportional rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "fe83e8c9-948a-596f-a2d9-c2ae2fe4f335" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6890 :tutorial/title "Determinants with Proportional Rows/Columns"} :step/id #uuid "23e26677-bdeb-5a45-a6d3-4a8d02a72732" :step/math-academy-id 41750 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134905}} {:db/id 17592186134905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133912 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133467 :question/id #uuid "dc780837-b763-5ba9-981a-2373afcb524a" :question/math-academy-id "e-10995"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8aef330a-81b3-56c4-9559-67df673e8687" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134394} {:db/id 17592186134407} {:db/id 17592186272011} {:db/id 17592186329654} {:db/id 17592186351409} {:db/id 17592186402861} {:db/id 17592186402868} {:db/id 17592186411852} {:db/id 17592186415475} {:db/id 17592186415477} {:db/id 17592186415478}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Determinant of a Matrix With Two Proportional Rows/Columns"} :step/id #uuid "93111f5e-5fd2-5a5b-81b1-27969a9b5d1d" :step/math-academy-id 41751 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134906}} {:db/id 17592186134906 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135154 :tutorial/content "In conclusion, if an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ satisfies any one of the following conditions, then $\det(A)=0.$

- $A$ has a zero row/column

- $A$ has two identical rows/columns

- $A$ has two proportional rows/columns

- $A$ has a row/column that is a linear combination of other rows/columns

Notice that condition IV encompasses each of the conditions I, II, and III. If we have a zero row/column, two identical rows/columns, or proportional rows/columns, then the rows/columns form a linearly dependent set of vectors. 
In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

**Watch out!** While all of the above conditions are *sufficient* to conclude that $\det(A)=0,$ only condition IV is *necessary* to conclude that $\det(A)=0.$ 
In other words, if we have a matrix $A$ with $\det(A)=0,$ then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV *must* be satisfied. 

So, we have the following theorem:

*$\det(A)=0$ if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

Finally, note also that in the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix *only*, statements III and IV mean the same thing." :tutorial/id #uuid "9d8b0323-170c-5a60-b372-1a258c4848cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6891 :tutorial/title "Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero"} :step/id #uuid "4aec093b-050b-5263-9ef2-c875455b8c07" :step/math-academy-id 41754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134908}} {:db/id 17592186134907 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133913 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133468 :question/id #uuid "33ca37e5-c598-52a2-861f-2d5bfa6fd571" :question/math-academy-id "e-10996"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abaeea03-6a2a-5d37-a2af-a9ea109175ad" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134393} {:db/id 17592186134414} {:db/id 17592186272012} {:db/id 17592186272013} {:db/id 17592186329652} {:db/id 17592186329653} {:db/id 17592186329699} {:db/id 17592186351410} {:db/id 17592186415476} {:db/id 17592186415479} {:db/id 17592186420353}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Reasons Why a Determinant Equals Zero"} :step/id #uuid "81571aa7-ce3d-5713-bf67-a49538fee0ef" :step/math-academy-id 41755} {:db/id 17592186134908 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135155 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. 

For example:

- Suppose the columns of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}}, {\color{black}\mathbf{b}},$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{c}}.$
![](images/6e/6e046341b7a1b8f6760797f7db89a7e021a6ace6b5cdf28bd5217998cb450837.svg)
The $3$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $A$ is depicted below:

![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)

The volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(A)\right|
$$

- Now suppose the columns of a $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{q}}.$
![](images/f5/f593c123eb081da0399e74c665325774758b48c5f086a7475b959905e1de2763.svg)
The $2$-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ is shown below:

![](images/4a/4af1971404b188df75bb3d62d47ac95340c5e1791066e5358370d743230baa45.png)

The two-dimensional volume $V$ (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $B{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(B)\right|
$$

- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix $M$ gives the $n$-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $M.$

In this lesson, we studied the following property:

*$\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*

What does this property mean in geometric terms?

The component $\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. 

Consider the following examples:

- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a "flat" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.

- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f7191c6-60ca-5c44-befc-8dbad7779b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6893 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of a Zero Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "8c5dbeea-b2e4-5fe9-9d8c-98750164b70c" :step/math-academy-id 41766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134907}}] :activity/title "Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134042} {:db/id 17592186134901 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135151 :tutorial/content "If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

**Watch out!** While all of the above conditions are *sufficient* to conclude that $\det(A)=0,$ only condition IV is *necessary* to conclude that $\det(A)=0.$ 
In other words, if we have a matrix $A$ with $\det(A)=0,$ then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV *must* be satisfied. 

So, we have the following theorem:

*$\det(A)=0$ if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

Finally, note also that in the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix *only*, statements III and IV mean the same thing." :tutorial/id #uuid "9d8b0323-170c-5a60-b372-1a258c4848cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6891 :tutorial/title "Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero"} :step/id #uuid "4aec093b-050b-5263-9ef2-c875455b8c07" :step/math-academy-id 41754 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134908}} {:db/id 17592186135154 :tutorial/content "In conclusion, if an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ satisfies any one of the following conditions, then $\det(A)=0.$

Finally, note also that in the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix *only*, statements III and IV mean the same thing." :tutorial/id #uuid "9d8b0323-170c-5a60-b372-1a258c4848cc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6891 :tutorial/title "Conditions When a Determinant Equals Zero"} {:db/id 17592186134908 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135155 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. 

For example:

- Suppose the columns of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}}, {\color{black}\mathbf{b}},$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{c}}.$
![](images/6e/6e046341b7a1b8f6760797f7db89a7e021a6ace6b5cdf28bd5217998cb450837.svg)
The $3$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $A$ is depicted below:

![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)

The volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(A)\right|
$$

- Now suppose the columns of a $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{q}}.$
![](images/f5/f593c123eb081da0399e74c665325774758b48c5f086a7475b959905e1de2763.svg)
The $2$-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ is shown below:

![](images/4a/4af1971404b188df75bb3d62d47ac95340c5e1791066e5358370d743230baa45.png)

The two-dimensional volume $V$ (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $B{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(B)\right|
$$

- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix $M$ gives the $n$-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $M.$

In this lesson, we studied the following property:

*$\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*

What does this property mean in geometric terms?

The component $\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. 

Consider the following examples:

- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a "flat" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.

- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "1f7191c6-60ca-5c44-befc-8dbad7779b08" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6893 :tutorial/title "Geometric Interpretation of a Zero Determinant"} :step/id #uuid "8c5dbeea-b2e4-5fe9-9d8c-98750164b70c" :step/math-academy-id 41766 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134907}} {:db/id 17592186134907 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133913 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133468 :question/id #uuid "33ca37e5-c598-52a2-861f-2d5bfa6fd571" :question/math-academy-id "e-10996"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "abaeea03-6a2a-5d37-a2af-a9ea109175ad" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134393} {:db/id 17592186134414} {:db/id 17592186272012} {:db/id 17592186272013} {:db/id 17592186329652} {:db/id 17592186329653} {:db/id 17592186329699} {:db/id 17592186351410} {:db/id 17592186415476} {:db/id 17592186415479} {:db/id 17592186420353}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying the Reasons Why a Determinant Equals Zero"} :step/id #uuid "81571aa7-ce3d-5713-bf67-a49538fee0ef" :step/math-academy-id 41755} {:db/id 17592186135155 :tutorial/content "Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant.

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ has a zero column
- **II.** $A$ has two proportional rows
- **III.** One of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.

- Statements I and II are false. For example, consider the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Expending across the $1$st column, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-2)+(1-2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

but $A$ has neither a zero column nor two proportional rows.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only"."} :step/id #uuid "73a434b3-1e72-5102-a3b4-f3e485e5088a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415482}} {:db/id 17592186415482 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415475 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "045918a8-9cd8-5a07-b550-ae46024d9091" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$|A|$ and $|C|$ only" :db/id 17592186415446} {:answer/id #uuid "402ee237-56af-5ed0-b68b-15a4eb93a4c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$|B|$ and $|C|$ only" :db/id 17592186415451} {:answer/id #uuid "82c9a685-f3be-5652-9e92-444a23e21632" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$|A|$ and $|B|$ only" :db/id 17592186415458} {:answer/id #uuid "f5705fa2-288d-561a-9ae0-435e05884593" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$|A|,$ $|B|,$ and $|C|$" :db/id 17592186415466} {:answer/id #uuid "fff98d8e-e1e9-59ce-9f45-62d4096f2b19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "$|C|$ only" :db/id 17592186415469}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415466} :answer-field/id #uuid "3898e8c8-305f-5107-8e55-3fa0057b225c" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415470}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "135c5d03-e391-5a5b-8227-7d54c7203318" :question/math-academy-id "q-140048" :question/problem "Which of the following determinants are equal to $0?$

$$
|A|=|\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}|,\,|B|=|\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & 2 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} & 1\end{aligned}|,\,|C|=|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}|
$$" :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the given determinants in turn.

- Since $A$ is a triangular matrix, its determinant is given by the product of the elements of the main diagonal:

$$
|A|=0\cdot 0\cdot 0\cdot 0=0
$$

- The matrix $B$ has proportional rows: 

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & \sqrt{2} & 1 \\ \sqrt{2} & 2 & \sqrt{2} \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 
As a result, $|B|=0.$

- The matrix $C$ has a zero column: 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 5 \\ -1 & 0 & 3 \\ 2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

As a result, $|C|=0.$

Therefore, $|A|,$ $|B|,$ and $|C|$ are equal to $0.$"} :step/id #uuid "7fde0eea-1a95-5e36-bc1d-53171442da99"} {:db/id 17592186415483 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415478 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1859d7c5-0d55-5273-a004-f8368886466b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186415448} {:answer/id #uuid "4a61a420-d52d-5f1a-b48b-ade03dffdca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186415453} {:answer/id #uuid "5fcc61bd-b9ee-5f9e-8558-651f8ea9c858" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186415454} {:answer/id #uuid "851dc3ec-467b-568b-a964-3b5e34b3527e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12" :db/id 17592186415459} {:answer/id #uuid "e2e4e722-717d-508c-a98d-112f70b09d9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18" :db/id 17592186415463}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415463} :answer-field/id #uuid "f920ea7f-06a7-52e9-8586-d0e6b44af6b3" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415474}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e897ce2c-45dd-5cf3-9d25-ca84c0dd6ea8" :question/math-academy-id "q-42881" :question/problem "Find $3det(A)-det(B)$, where

A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2.05 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & \sqrt{7} & 2\end{aligned}]

Consider the matrix given above. Identify **all** of the reasons why one can conclude that $|A|=0?$
- **I.** $A$ has proportional columns
- **II.** $A$ has identical rows
- **III.** $A$ has a zero row

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- $A$ has proportional columns: 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2.05 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 6 & \sqrt{7} & 2\end{aligned}]\,✓
$$

- $A$ does *not* have identical rows.

$$

- **III.** $A$ does not have proportional columns

- Statement I is false. For example, consider the matrix 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
|A|=1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot 2=5\ne 0
$$

but $A$ is not a triangular matrix.

- Statements II and III are true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$|A|=0$ *if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

In the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix, this means that one of the rows/columns must be proportional to another row/column.
Hence, if $|A|\ne 0$ then $A$ doesn't have proportional nor identical rows/columns.

$$

17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f8a11ae3-b740-5975-a251-a4796d69b742" :question/math-academy-id "q-43307" :question/problem "Let $A$ be a $3\times 3$ matrix such that $|A|=0.$ Which of the following statements must be true?

- **I.** $A$ has a zero column
- **II.** $A$ has two proportional rows
- **III.** One of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A$" :question/worked-solution "Let's consider our statements in turn.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A| & =1\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}|+1|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(3-2)+(1-2) \\  & =0\end{aligned}

but $A$ has neither a zero column nor two proportional rows.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, we can make use of the following fact:

$$
\begin{aligned}
(6x^{2} + x + 1) + (2x^{2} - 3x + 6) &=  \\

6x^{2} + 2x^{2}_(⏟)_(x^{2}terms) + x - 3x^(⏞)^(xterms) + 1 + 6_(⏟)_(constants) &=  \\
(6 + 2)x^{2} + (1 - 3)x + 7 &=  \\
&= 8x^{2} - 2x + 7
\end{aligned}

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the global maximum of the function $f(x,y)=2{e}^{xy-x}$ on the closed triangular region  $D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2-x}.$ You're given that $f$ has a critical point at $(0,1)$ and on the boundary of the triangle the points that could give rise to extreme values are the vertices and the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

To determine the critical points, let's first sketch the region:

![](images/42/42b9bcda74e29cf7012fd9576ee7bcea92bfc3f58fab4c43c854892afe3acc44.png)

 

Since the point $(0,1)$ does not belong to the interior of $D$, we do not yet include it in the list of candidates for extrema (it lies on the boundary of $D,$ so we will consider it in the next step).

**Step 2.** Find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values. 

In this case, we are *given* the points on the boundary of our region that could potentially be global extrema for $f.$ These are

$$
(0,0),\,(2,0),\,(0,1),\,(0,2),\,(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2})
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2{e}^{(0)(0)-(0)} \\  & =2 \\ f(2,0) & =2{e}^{(2)(0)-(2)} \\  & =2{e}^{-2} \\ f(0,1) & =2{e}^{(0)(1)-(0)} \\  & =2 \\ f(0,2) & =2{e}^{(0)(2)-(0)} \\  & =2 \\ f(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}) & =2{e}^{(1/2)(3/2)-(1/2)} \\  & =2\sqrt[4]{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $2{e}^{-2}$ at the point $(2,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $2\sqrt[4]{e}$ at the point $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186404350 :question/id #uuid "32f5ebff-a024-5f63-b943-142f3a504252" critical point at $(0,-3),$ and on the boundary of the region the points that could give rise to extreme values are $(-2,-4),$ $(-1,-1),$ $(1,-1),$ and $(2,-4).$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

**Step 1.** Find the critical points inside the region $D.$ 

To determine the critical points, let's first sketch the region:

![](images/96/96096b5f8944785f1af1bbc4fd4942e081b4b3999887c0fa8d5d76008af454d5.png)

Since the point $(0,-3)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.** Find the points on the boundary that could give rise to extreme values.

In this case, we are *given* the points on the boundary of our region that could potentially be global extrema for $f.$ These are

$$
(-2,-4),\,(-1,-1),\,(1,-1),\,(2,-4).
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,-3) & =2(0)(-3)+6(0)-3 \\  & =-3 \\ f(-2,-4) & =2(-2)(-4)+6(-2)-3 \\  & =1 \\ f(-1,-1) & =2(-1)(-1)+6(-1)-3 \\  & =-7 \\ f(1,-1) & =2(1)(-1)+6(1)-3 \\  & =1 \\ f(2,-4) & =2(2)(-4)+6(2)-3 \\  & =-7\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-7$ at the points $(-1,-1)$ and $(2,-4),$

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $1$ at the points $(-2,-4)$ and $(1,-1).$"} {:db/id 17592186404371 :question/id #uuid "24be252f-8729-57e6-8082-158ca3588445" :question/math-academy-id "q-86724"} $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4x+4$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 9}.$ You are given that the function has a critical point at $(2,0)\in D.$" :question/worked-solution "Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ that lie inside the region $D.$ 

We have been given that $f$ has a critical point at 

$\,$ $(2,0)$ 

which belongs to the interior of the region $D.$ So, we include this point in the list of candidates for the extrema. 

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}-4(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+4 \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t+9{sin}^{2}⁡t-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4 \\  & =13-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (13-12\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{′} & =0 \\ 12\operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡t & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation gives one solution $t=\pi \in (0,2\pi ).$
We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can possibly give rise to extreme values are $t=0,\,\pi .$ Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain two candidate points:

$$
(3,0),\,(-3,0)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Let's compare the values of $f(x,y)$ evaluated at each of the points mentioned above. 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,0) & =(2)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(2)+4 \\  & =4+0-8+4 \\  & =0 \\ f(3,0) & =(3)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(3)+4 \\  & =9+0-12+4 \\  & =1 \\ f(-3,0) & =(-3)^{2}+(0)^{2}-4(-3)+4 \\  & =9+0+12+4 \\  & =25\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $0$ at the point $(2,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $25$ at the point $(-3,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186125064 :question/id #uuid "784d8995-a39a-5567-b522-960291c7a1e9" :question/math-academy-id "q-37372"} {:db/id :topic/math-academy-id 1947} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125655 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125892 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the **global maximum** and **global minimum** of a function $f(x,y).$ Recall that the global maximum and minimum of a function are collectively known as **global extrema.** 

The procedure we will describe for finding the global extrema is based on a general principle called the **extreme-value theorem,** which states the following:

*Every function that is continuous on a closed, bounded region $D$ has global extrema (i.e., both a global maximum and a global minimum) on $D$*.

Let's consider the function $f(x,y) =  e^{x^2- y^2}$ on the closed  region $D=\{(x,y)\in \mathbb R^2: \,  x^2 +y^2  \leq 1\}.$ How do we find the global extrema?

To find the global extrema of a differentiable function on a closed, bounded region $D,$ we follow these steps:

**Step 1**:  Determine the critical points of $f$ in the interior of $D.$

![](images/50/5057a4a96daa4819a70e733519c89802c28bde184183db2b4efbe69d3db36e56.png)

To determine the critical points, we solve $\boldsymbol f' = \mathbf 0.$ Computing the derivative gives

![](images/b4/b48de1dcd3a240a1f1904dd290ef0665fc603c4cc5f99915915c6a12f79d74d9.svg)

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}2x{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0 \\ -2y{e}^{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

This gives us a single point $(0,0).$ Since the point $(0,0)$ is in the interior of $D,$ we include it in the list of candidates for extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of ${D}$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle $x^2 + y^2 =1.$ This gives

$$
\mathbf{r} = \langle \cos{t}, \sin{t} \rangle, \qquad t \in [0,2\pi).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & ={e}^{{cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t \in (0,2\pi),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ ({e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)})^{′} & =0 \\ -2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t){e}^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has three solutions, namely 

$$
t =\dfrac\pi 2, \: \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}2 \in (0,2\pi).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval, namely, $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \:  \pi, \: \dfrac{3\pi}{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ for each value of $t$, we obtain the following candidate points:

$$
(1,0), \: (0,1), \: (-1,0), \: (0,-1)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values.

Evaluating $f$ at the five points we've found gives the following table of values:

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(1,0)$ | $(0,1)$ | $(-1,0)$ | $(0,-1)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $e$ | $1/e$ | $e$ | $1/e$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $\dfrac1e$ at the points $(0,1), \, (0,-1),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $e$ at the points $(1,0), \, (-1,0).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b8b379fb-f7e4-5cdb-b25a-69a6c2ae9cf2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7879 :tutorial/title "Introduction"}
